title: Conversational Artificial Intelligence in Customer Service: Technological Foundations, User Experience, and Ethical Considerations
abstract: Modern software capable of holding a conversation has quietly become one of the defining tools of contemporary client-facing operations. Built on progress in language understanding models, statistical learning, and computational reasoning, these programs can grasp what a person is asking for, reply in a way that fits the situation, and keep working around the clock across many different platforms at once. Because they can absorb the bulk of repetitive requests, companies rely on them to ease staffing pressure while still offering the kind of tailored response that keeps people coming back. The reach of this shift goes past simple cost savings, it is quietly rearranging how firms store and use institutional knowledge, how choices get made internally, and what staff actually spend their working hours doing, as routine exchanges move to software and people are freed up for work that calls for judgment.Alongside these gains sit real difficulties that cannot be waved away, questions about how personal information is handled, the risk of skewed or unfair replies, the murkiness of how a given answer was produced, and the challenge of building one system that serves wildly different audiences equally well. Tackling these problems calls for oversight put in place ahead of time rather than bolted on afterward, design choices that account for a broad range of users from the start, and evaluation that never really stops. On a more constructive note, the huge volume of exchanges these systems record turns into a genuine resource for understanding what customers actually want, letting firms act before a problem surfaces, sharpen what they recommend, and base choices on observed patterns instead of guesswork.Looking forward, worthwhile lines of inquiry include richer conversational designs, a sharper picture of how people and software negotiate trust, closer ties with neighboring technologies, and studies that track outcomes well beyond a single launch window. The overall picture that emerges is one where raw technical power on its own is not enough, durable value comes from combining that power with attentiveness to the person on the other end of the conversation, which is what turns a support tool into a genuine engine of organizational change rather than a cosmetic upgrade.

title: A scalable AI framework for automated TNM staging of 51,242 patients with nasopharyngeal carcinoma
abstract: Accurate tumor-node-metastasis (TNM) staging is essential for treatment decision-making, prognostic stratification, and outcomes modeling in oncology. However, real-world clinical databases often extend over decades and inherently encompass multiple successive staging systems, introducing substantial heterogeneity that undermines the stability and interpretability of survival analyses, prognostic modeling, and staging system evaluation. To address this challenge, we developed an automated framework that combines TNM staging criteria and staging-relevant anatomical knowledge with a large language model (LLM) and a second-stage reflection step to convert narrative radiology reports into unified AJCC/UICC 9th edition TNM staging. In an expert-annotated cohort of 340 NPC patients, we evaluated multiple LLMs and found that the GLM4.5-based framework achieved the highest accuracy for T (0.95), N (0.86), and M (0.99) classification. Based on this optimal performance, the framework was applied to a real-world cohort of 51,242 NPC patients between 2010 and 2025. A stratified random validation subset of 200 cases showed high concordance with the expert reference standard. In downstream utility analyses, the unified staging was associated with a higher C-index and more distinct survival-curve separation than existing electronic health record staging. Collectively, this study provides a scalable framework for unifying heterogeneous historical cancer staging data, supporting longitudinal analyses in large real-world oncology cohorts.

title: RRWK: structural and computational bounds for dense graph subgraph extraction
abstract: Subgraph extraction constitutes a key component of graph representation learning, enabling scalable analysis and downstream inference over large and complex networks. Nevertheless, existing local extraction approaches frequently exhibit substantial performance degradation in dense graph regimes, where excessive neighborhood expansion and the loss of structural cohesion negatively affect both computational tractability and representational fidelity. Recent work has reformulated the subgraph extraction task in this problem as a local clustering procedure based on a personalized PageRank. However, despite obtaining better results, this approach is affected by the density of the network, limiting its results to networks with medium-low density. In this work, we introduce return random walk kinship (RRWK), a density-aware subgraph extraction framework based on bounded outbound and return random-walk connectivity. The proposed method preserves structurally cohesive regions by exploiting alternative return paths capable of jointly capturing local and global organizational properties of the graph. In contrast to conventional enclosing-subgraph and personalized PageRank-based strategies, RRWK is specifically designed to maintain structural robustness as graph density increases. Furthermore, we study the structural and computational bounds of the proposed method. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that RRWK consistently preserves the structural properties of the original graph more accurately than state-of-the-art subgraph extraction baselines, while maintaining competitive computational performance in dense graph scenarios.

title: CoMLP: Cooperatively-Gated MLPs for Fine-Grained Cross-Modal Information Fusion in Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Multi-modal medical images and clinical reports provide complementary anatomical, functional, and semantic information for medical image segmentation. Effectively exploiting these heterogeneous sources requires fine-grained cross-modal information fusion that preserves subtle spatial details while capturing semantic dependencies across modalities. Existing fusion approaches frequently rely on cross-attention, whose computational burden increases rapidly with spatial resolution, making dense cross-modal interaction difficult on high-resolution feature maps, particularly for volumetric medical images. In this work, we propose CoMLP, a cooperatively-gated MLP module for fine-grained cross-modal information fusion in medical image segmentation. CoMLP models cross-modal dependencies through cooperative cross-gating, built upon complementary regional and dilated MLP interactions, to capture local and global cross-modal dependencies. We further develop a multi-source fusion architecture in which CoMLP performs both inter-image fusion across imaging modalities and vision-language fusion between visual features and textual reports, enabling heterogeneous information to be integrated without relying on dense cross-attention. Extensive experiments on five medical segmentation benchmarks, covering 2D/3D images, clinical reports, multiple imaging modalities, and diverse anatomical regions, demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art multi-modal and language-guided segmentation methods. Ablation studies further show that fine-grained interaction at high spatial resolutions and complementary local-global fusion are critical to the performance gains. These results demonstrate the potential of MLP-based interaction as an effective alternative for fine-grained cross-modal information fusion in medical image segmentation.

title: Multi-Scale Quantum Topology Analysis
abstract: This paper explores the application of quantum topology to analyze complex quantum systems, focusing on the identification and prediction of their behavior across multiple scales. We propose a novel theoretical framework that integrates quantum entanglement and topological geometry to construct a model capable of simultaneously assessing diverse quantum topology structures. The core mechanism involves establishing a dynamic, multi-scale model that predicts emergent phenomena based on the interplay of these structural elements. This research aims to provide a robust theoretical foundation for quantum computing and information processing, offering a potential path towards more accurate and efficient quantum algorithms and devices.

title: Quantum Geometry and Quantum Computation via Spin-Based Non-Euclidean Structures
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of utilizing quantum spin properties to develop novel non-Euclidean geometric structures, with the aim of enhancing the efficiency of quantum computation. We explore the design of a quantum geometry framework predicated on these spin properties, proposing specific quantum algorithms that capitalize on the inherent advantages of spin dynamics within the framework. The core mechanism centers around constructing a basis for non-Euclidean geometry through the manipulation of spin states, leading to improved computational capabilities. This work presents a conceptual framework and outlines preliminary considerations for leveraging quantum spin phenomena to advance quantum algorithm design and computational efficiency.

title: Dynamically Generated Quantum Error Correction Codes
abstract: Quantum computation holds immense promise for scientific breakthroughs and technological advancements, but the inherent fragility of quantum states necessitates robust error correction. Current error correction protocols, while effective, are often computationally intensive and limited by the complexity of the error correction codes themselves. This paper explores a novel approach leveraging dynamically generated quantum error correction codes to enhance the fidelity of quantum computations. We propose a quantum circuit architecture that generates error correction codes based on the current state of the computation, dynamically adjusting the code complexity. This dynamic adjustment aims to mitigate the computational burden associated with traditional error correction methods, paving the way for more efficient and scalable quantum systems.

title: 异构量子计算的概率分布建模
abstract: 异构量子计算,作为一种新兴的量子计算技术,具有巨大的潜力,但其可靠性和稳定性仍然是一个关键挑战。传统的量子计算模型往往难以准确地捕捉量子计算的随机性,而这种捕捉的不足是导致量子计算可靠性下降的主要原因。本研究提出了一种基于异构量子计算的概率分布建模框架,旨在将量子计算的随机性与经典计算的稳定性结合起来,从而提高量子计算的可靠性和稳定性。本文详细阐述了该框架的设计思路、关键步骤和潜在应用,并对未来的研究方向进行了展望。

title: Adaptive Topology Deformation of High-Dimensional Geometric Topology & Quantum Algorithm Fusion
abstract: This paper investigates the application of adaptive topology deformation techniques, combined with quantum algorithms, to enhance geometric transformations and computational efficiency in high-dimensional spaces. We introduce a novel algorithm that dynamically adjusts topology based on input data, leveraging quantum processing to achieve unprecedented precision in geometric reconstruction and manipulation. The core of this approach centers around a self-organizing topology framework, enabling the algorithm to effectively bridge the gap between traditional geometric methods and the capabilities of quantum computation. The study focuses on demonstrating the algorithm's effectiveness in tasks requiring precise geometric transformations, specifically addressing challenges in data analysis and simulation within complex high-dimensional environments. This research explores the potential of quantum-enhanced topology for significantly accelerating geometric processes, offering a paradigm shift in computational geometry.

title: The Convergence of Optimization and Geometry: A Novel Approach to Machine Learning Model Tuning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel machine learning algorithm, termed "Adaptive Geometry Optimization," designed to mitigate the reliance on data distribution during model training. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with complex models exhibiting intricate dependencies. This algorithm dynamically adjusts geometric constraints to guide the optimization process, leading to improved model performance and robustness. The core mechanism involves transforming machine learning model constraints and data distributions into a self-adaptive geometric framework, enabling fine-grained parameter optimization. This approach offers a more flexible and potentially more effective method for tuning complex models, particularly in scenarios where data distribution is a significant challenge. The proposed algorithm demonstrates improved convergence and generalization performance compared to existing techniques, establishing a new foundation for optimizing machine learning models.

title: Quantum Machine Learning for Adaptive Topological Structure Prediction
abstract: This paper explores the application of quantum machine learning to the prediction of complex topological structures. Traditional machine learning methods often struggle with the inherent complexity and high dimensionality of topological data, requiring extensive feature engineering and potentially leading to suboptimal model performance. Quantum machine learning offers the potential to address these challenges by leveraging quantum phenomena to efficiently represent and process information, enabling the prediction of intricate topological landscapes. We propose a novel quantum algorithm designed to learn a predictive model based on the underlying topological structure, incorporating this information to enhance predictive accuracy. The core mechanism focuses on utilizing quantum state manipulation to capture the essential relationships within the topology, resulting in a more robust and accurate prediction. The research investigates the potential of this approach to significantly improve the prediction of topological structures, particularly for complex and high-dimensional datasets.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Continual Learning via Adaptive Rule Induction
abstract: Continual learning (CL) presents a significant challenge in artificial intelligence: the ability of a model to learn continuously from a stream of data without forgetting previously acquired knowledge. Traditional approaches often rely on either catastrophic forgetting mitigation strategies or knowledge distillation, each with limitations. This paper proposes a novel neuro-symbolic continual learning architecture that addresses these shortcomings by dynamically integrating new knowledge through adaptive rule induction. The system combines the representation learning capabilities of neural networks with the explicit reasoning power of symbolic rules. The core claim is that a system can learn continuously by actively inducing and refining symbolic rules. This is achieved through a rule induction engine guided by uncertainty and consistency metrics, ensuring that new rules are generated based on the current learned representation and that existing rules are adapted to maintain overall system coherence. The mechanism leverages neural networks to learn representations from each task, while the rule induction engine generates and updates symbolic rules based on these representations. The system's adaptability allows it to effectively handle the temporal dynamics inherent in continual learning scenarios. This approach moves beyond simple knowledge transfer and establishes a mechanism for the system to actively integrate new information into its symbolic understanding, representing a crucial step towards truly intelligent and adaptive AI systems.

title: 基于动态的量子纠缠的概率建模
abstract: This paper introduces a novel probabilistic modeling approach for quantum entanglement, leveraging dynamic quantum entanglement states. Traditional methods often rely on static models, limiting the system's adaptability. This work proposes a method where the entangled state itself acts as the model parameter, enabling dynamic adjustments that improve the accuracy of quantum computations. We explore a mechanism to iteratively refine the entanglement state based on environmental changes, achieving a significant improvement in computational fidelity. This advancement offers a promising path toward more robust and versatile quantum algorithms.

title: Quantum State Dynamic Mapping and Optimization for Quantum Computing
abstract: Quantum state dynamic mapping is a promising approach for optimizing quantum computation. This paper explores a novel method leveraging dynamic adjustment of quantum states to enhance the performance of quantum algorithms. We propose a framework combining quantum state evolution with optimization algorithms to achieve significant improvements. The core mechanism centers on dynamically adjusting parameters to guide the quantum state towards optimal configurations, ultimately boosting computational capabilities. This work offers a potential paradigm shift in quantum algorithm design and optimization, moving beyond traditional static optimization techniques.

title: Neural Symbolic Fusion Algorithm (NBF)
abstract: Neural Symbolic Fusion Algorithm (NBF) presents a novel approach to model interpretation and reasoning by integrating the strengths of neural networks and symbolic reasoning. This algorithm leverages a unique fusion mechanism that simultaneously learns patterns from neural networks and applies symbolic rules for inference, resulting in enhanced model explainability and accuracy. This work introduces a new methodology that overcomes the limitations of traditional approaches by providing a more comprehensive and robust modeling framework.

title: Quantum Entanglement in a Non-Classical Computing Paradigm
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a bizarre phenomenon where two or more particles become inextricably linked, holds immense promise for revolutionizing computation. This paper explores the potential of utilizing quantum entanglement to develop a novel computing paradigm, termed "Quantum Entanglement-Driven Computation" (QEDC). We propose a model centered around a 'correlations' calculation framework, leveraging entanglement for information processing and data encoding. The core mechanism focuses on establishing a dynamic relationship between classical and quantum systems, enabling exponential computational capabilities. This approach aims to overcome the limitations of classical computing by effectively utilizing entanglement to perform calculations beyond the reach of conventional algorithms. The research highlights the potential for QEDC to address key challenges in computational complexity and information security.

title: Adaptive Quantum Simulation Parameter Adjustment
abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive quantum simulation parameter adjustment method designed to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of quantum simulations. Traditional approaches often rely on fixed parameters, while this work leverages dynamic parameter adjustments within quantum simulation to achieve superior results. We detail the core mechanism, outlining how the simulation process iteratively refines parameters based on observed results, ultimately optimizing for the desired level of fidelity. This approach addresses limitations of existing methods, offering a novel pathway to improved simulation performance.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Driven Algorithmic Complexity Reduction
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a bizarre yet powerful quantum phenomenon, offers a tantalizing prospect for revolutionizing computationally intensive tasks. This research explores the potential of utilizing entanglement to dramatically reduce the computational complexity of complex optimization problems, with a particular focus on combinatorial optimization and machine learning. We propose a novel algorithm, guided by quantum entanglement, that employs a modified Grover's algorithm enhanced with quantum entanglement to achieve exponential speedups. The core mechanism centers around creating entangled qubit states to represent potential solutions and enabling efficient search and evaluation. This paper details the theoretical framework, algorithm design, and preliminary results demonstrating the potential of this approach. The implications of this work extend beyond simple speedups, potentially opening avenues for fundamentally new algorithmic paradigms.

title: Nonlinear Quantum Entanglement Self-Adaptation Topology
abstract: This paper introduces a novel algorithm based on nonlinear quantum entanglement to dynamically adjust the topology of a quantum system. The core principle lies in exploiting the inherent properties of entangled states to induce and control topological changes, leading to enhanced computational and modeling capabilities. The algorithm's strength stems from its self-adaptive nature, allowing for continuous optimization and the potential to overcome limitations of traditional topological methods. This work explores the potential of this approach, demonstrating its efficacy through theoretical analysis and preliminary experimental validation. The proposed method addresses the challenge of designing robust and flexible topology, offering a pathway towards more powerful quantum computations and simulations.

title: Generative AI and Project Risk Management: Human-AI Collaboration Under Uncertainty
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly entering project-management activities that involve large volumes of unstructured information, uncertain conditions, and consequential managerial judgment. Project risk management is a particularly important setting because AI may help project teams identify risks, synthesize dispersed evidence, generate scenarios, and formulate response alternatives, yet the consequences of misplaced reliance can be substantial. This integrative literature review develops a process-based framework for human-GenAI collaboration in project risk management. The framework links project risk information to GenAI-assisted risk identification, GenAI-supported assessment and scenario analysis, human verification and contextual interpretation, human-AI response development, human accountable choice, and monitoring and feedback. The article further distinguishes AI capability from AI authority and proposes four interacting dimensions for determining appropriate GenAI authority: uncertainty, risk consequences, verifiability, and managerial expertise. A four-level authority continuum is introduced, ranging from informational support to delegated decision authority. The synthesis suggests that high uncertainty can increase the value of GenAI for exploration while simultaneously reducing the justification for autonomous AI choice. The article concludes that successful adoption should be evaluated through the quality of the human-AI decision architecture rather than the amount of human work replaced. Keywords: generative artificial intelligence, project risk management, human-AI collaboration, uncertainty, decision authority, risk governance, managerial judgment

title: Discovering disease risk trends by applying Latent Dirichlet Allocation sentiment analysis to social media health discussions
abstract: Social media platforms generate large volumes of health-related content that can provide valuable insights into emerging disease concerns and public perceptions. This study explores disease-risk trends through topic modeling and sentiment analysis of social media discussions. We used Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) to extract topics and VADER sentiments from 50,000 statements related to diseases. The model performance was evaluated in terms of coherence, topic diversity, and stability metrics. The comparison was made with NMF and BERTopic. Three main topics were identified: COVID-19 symptoms and diagnosis; chronic disease management; and disease risk factors. The LDA model obtained coherence and topic diversity scores of 0.402 and 0.77, respectively. The sentiment analysis shows that the discussions are overall neutral, with some sentiments related to negative concerns. The results indicate that the use of topic modeling along with sentiment analysis is a useful approach to extract major disease-related topics from social media data. Future studies using transformer-based models, multilingual data, and longitudinal studies may improve digital disease surveillance and enable proactive public health monitoring.

title: Data Scout: Targeted Web Crawling for Domain-Specific Pretraining Corpora
abstract: The dominant approach to building domain-specific pretraining corpora is to filter large web archives such as CommonCrawl. This works well for popular domains but breaks down for specialized ones, where relevant content is sparse and often beyond the reach of popularity-driven crawlers. We present Data Scout, which inverts this: instead of filtering an archive, it directs a targeted crawl. An LLM expands a root topic into a taxonomy and thousands of search queries; the returned URLs (seeds) are grouped by subdomain and screened with a user-supplied classifier (the probe), admitting each subdomain on the basis of a small sample. This works because relevance has a sharp boundary at the subdomain level: in mathematics, a page is 21x more likely to be relevant than one on a sibling subdomain. With the FineMath classifier as the probe, 21.9% of crawled pages are high-quality math content, 70x the 0.31% rate from filtering a comparable web sample, so the crawl wastes far less effort. But the payoff is not just efficiency: 63.2% of these pages are missing from CommonCrawl altogether, yet just as useful for training. Continued pretraining of Llama-3.2-3B on 1.9B Data Scout tokens matches FineMath corpus on GSM8k. Because the probe is the only domain-specific component, Data Scout can in principle apply to any domain with such a classifier.

title: AUGUR: The Effective Epistemic Date of Time-Locked Language Models
abstract: A language model trained on nothing published after 1938, asked what year it is, answers 1899. Research groups are training language models from scratch on corpora that stop at a fixed historical date, on the assumption that a model with a 1938 cutoff represents 1938. This work measures that assumption and finds it wrong. A knowledge cutoff describes the edge of a training corpus, not its centre of gravity, and the two models tested both answer from four to eight decades before their stated cutoff when left unprompted. The work introduces the effective epistemic date: the year a model speaks from when nobody tells it otherwise. It further shows that recoverability is a second, independent axis. Given a one-sentence date anchor, one model relocates forty years on the spot and correctly names Herbert Hoover, his 1928 election and his inauguration date; the other does not move at all and confabulates instead. The practical rule that follows is to anchor the date and then verify the anchor took, because on half the models tested it did not. A second finding emerged from the demonstration: asked whether another great war was coming, a 1930-anchored model calls it highly improbable, while the same model in the same year, asked instead to enumerate the dangers facing Europe, produces an accurate threat assessment naming the Rhineland, Poland and Czechoslovakia. Both answers were present in the corpus. The form of the question decides which 1930 you meet, which makes elicitation part of the measurement rather than a neutral window onto it. Scope and limits: n = 2 model families. This is replication, not a law. Parameter count and quantisation are confounded with corpus composition and are not controlled. Both models also hallucinate forward, producing post-cutoff dates without post-cutoff knowledge, which means contamination checks that scan outputs for future years will produce false positives on them. Repository contains the full probe battery (14 probes, temperature 0, fixed seed), unedited raw model output for both models, the reproduction script, and the original plan including the forecasting programme that the first phase falsified.

title: Dynamic Adaptive Machine Learning Framework
abstract: This paper introduces a novel machine learning framework, termed the Dynamic Adaptive Machine Learning Framework (DAMLF), designed to enhance model generalization and adaptability by dynamically adjusting model parameters and training strategies. Traditional machine learning approaches often struggle to effectively handle data distribution heterogeneity, necessitating sophisticated parameter and strategy optimization. DAMFL leverages a mechanism that continuously adapts to the data's characteristics, mitigating overfitting and improving performance across diverse datasets. This paper details the framework's architecture, key algorithms, and validation results demonstrating its efficacy in several benchmark datasets.

title: Cognitive‑Temporal Technologies in the Carlo Field: A Full‑Max Engineering Blueprint for Thought‑Loop Compression, Memory‑Stability Fields, and Predictive Cognition Engines
abstract: This document establishes the complete engineering canon for **Cognitive‑Temporal Technologies (CTT)** — a new class of cognitive systems built on the Carlo Field. As stated in the document, “Cognitive systems interact with four Carlo operators,” enabling curvature‑shaped cognitive load modulation, temporal‑shear‑controlled processing speed, loop‑geometry‑based thought‑pattern stabilisation, and singularity‑aware prediction of mental‑state trajectories. Three flagship cognitive technologies are developed to maximal depth: - **Thought‑Loop Compressor (TLC):** Detects and collapses harmful cognitive loops such as rumination, recursive anxiety patterns, and runaway feedback dynamics using Carlo loop geometry and reset operators. - **Memory‑Stability Field (MSF):** Stabilises memory trajectories using curvature‑shaped recall potentials and temporal‑shear‑modulated consolidation rates, preventing memory collapse and enhancing recall stability. - **Predictive Cognition Engine (PCE):** Forecasts mental‑state trajectories using singularity geometry, enabling early detection of cognitive overload, panic collapse, and insight‑trajectory shaping. The document includes full mathematical operators, governing equations, device architectures, cognitive interface stacks, singularity‑avoidance constraints, and a complete roadmap for simulation, prototyping, and deployment. title: Title: Dynamic Recurrence Matrix (DRM)
abstract: Dynamic Recurrence Matrix (DRM) is a novel data analysis framework that utilizes iterative recurrence to automatically adapt to changing input data. This system learns a 'recurrence pattern' within the input data and adjusts the matrix structure to enhance accuracy and efficiency. The core mechanism revolves around the continuous refinement of the matrix, driven by an iterative process that optimizes performance. This approach represents a significant advancement over traditional data analysis methods, offering dynamic adaptability and improved results. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of DRM, detailing its theoretical underpinnings, the learning process, and the resulting benefits. The research explores the potential applications of DRM across diverse data domains, highlighting its capacity to address challenges associated with data drift and evolving patterns. The study also investigates the impact of different learning strategies on the system's performance, providing insights into the optimal configuration of the recurrence pattern. Finally, this paper discusses future research directions, aiming to expand the capabilities of DRM and solidify its position as a leading technique in data analysis.

title: Probability Geometry: A Quantum Theory of Geometric Quantization
abstract: This paper explores the application of probabilistic geometry to the theoretical framework of quantum computation, specifically focusing on the development of a quantum geometric quantization model. We propose a novel approach that integrates geometric structures and probabilistic logic to provide a deeper understanding of quantum systems and to guide the optimization of quantum algorithms. The core mechanism centers around representing quantum states as probability distributions, allowing for a more nuanced and robust analysis of quantum phenomena. This framework offers a new perspective on the design and analysis of quantum algorithms, potentially unlocking significant advancements in computational complexity.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Constraint Satisfaction with Adaptive Representation
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of quantum computing to enhance constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) through dynamic representation adjustment. CSPs are a fundamental problem in many areas of computer science and artificial intelligence, often exhibiting complex and unpredictable behavior. Traditional CSP solvers often struggle with large instances and intricate constraints. This research proposes a novel quantum algorithm designed to dynamically modify the representation of constraints, allowing for more efficient and robust exploration of solution spaces. We explore the use of quantum algorithms to create a representation that is inherently more flexible and resilient to variations in input data, leading to improved performance in solving complex CSPs. The paper details the underlying quantum mechanisms, discusses the potential benefits of this approach, and presents preliminary results demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method.

title: Self-Organizing Information Theory Quantum Entanglement Protocol
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum entanglement protocol based on self-organizing information theory. The protocol leverages the unique properties of quantum entanglement to ensure secure data transmission and synchronization, and explores its potential within quantum communication. The core mechanism focuses on utilizing the self-organizing information theory to achieve data security via entanglement, facilitate data compression and transfer through entanglement, and ultimately enhance communication efficiency and security. The investigation emphasizes the potential of this approach to overcome limitations in existing quantum communication methods.

title: Self-Adaptive Quantum Potential Optimization
abstract: Quantum computing is a rapidly advancing field with tremendous potential for scientific discovery and technological innovation. However, current quantum algorithms often suffer from limitations in scalability and robustness, hindering their widespread adoption. This paper introduces a novel approach to quantum potential optimization, leveraging the power of topology to create adaptable quantum systems. We explore the use of topological structures to design quantum potentials, effectively optimizing them to enhance quantum computation's efficiency and stability. The core mechanism involves constructing a topological structure that dynamically adjusts the quantum potential based on the specific characteristics of the target quantum system. This offers a promising path towards overcoming the challenges of traditional optimization techniques and enabling the development of more versatile and reliable quantum devices. This work is motivated by the inherent properties of topology and its ability to generate complex, self-similar patterns, suggesting a robust and adaptable framework for quantum system design. The presented methodology provides a new perspective on quantum potential optimization, opening avenues for enhanced device performance and broadened applicability.

The core mechanism centers around leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement to achieve precise matrix operations, complemented by a quantum simulation framework to enhance computational speed. The paper explores the potential applications of this method, highlighting its promise for overcoming limitations of classical computation in high-dimensional settings.

We propose a novel approach utilizing quantum entanglement and quantum simulation to accelerate calculations, offering a new avenue for solving problems across various fields, including optimization and materials science. The core mechanism centers around leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement to achieve precise matrix operations, complemented by a quantum simulation framework to enhance computational speed. The paper explores the potential applications of this method, highlighting its promise for overcoming limitations of classical computation in high-dimensional settings.

title: Based on Stream Computing Real-Time Anomaly Detection Algorithm
abstract: This paper presents a novel real-time anomaly detection algorithm based on stream computing. The algorithm leverages the characteristics of stream computing to process data streams in real-time and employs machine learning algorithms for anomaly identification. The core mechanism involves continuous monitoring of the data stream, immediate processing, and the application of predictive models to identify deviations from expected behavior. The proposed approach offers a significant improvement in response time compared to traditional batch-based anomaly detection methods, making it suitable for applications demanding immediate reaction to unusual events. This research addresses the challenges of latency and scalability inherent in real-time anomaly detection, providing a robust and efficient solution. The algorithm's performance is evaluated through simulated data streams, demonstrating its ability to accurately detect anomalies with minimal delay. The key contribution lies in the seamless integration of stream computing principles with machine learning, creating a dynamic and adaptive system for anomaly detection.

title: 基于自适应的量子机器学习算法的优化
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) offers the potential to revolutionize machine learning by leveraging the unique properties of quantum systems. However, scaling QML algorithms to complex problems remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces a novel quantum machine learning algorithm, termed Adaptive Quantum Optimization (AQO), designed to dynamically adjust quantum state parameters during training, thereby optimizing quantum model performance. The algorithm's core mechanism hinges on a self-adaptive optimization process, leveraging the inherent quantum properties to efficiently explore the parameter space and improve the accuracy and speed of quantum machine learning models. We demonstrate the efficacy of AQO through a series of theoretical analyses and preliminary experiments on a simplified quantum model, showcasing its ability to outperform conventional approaches in terms of convergence speed and model fidelity. The core claim is that AQO can significantly enhance the performance of quantum machine learning algorithms by dynamically optimizing quantum states.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Based Information Encoding Network
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to information processing by leveraging quantum entanglement within a neural network architecture. The core idea centers on encoding information within entangled quantum bits (qubits) and utilizing their correlated states for enhanced computational capabilities. Traditional neural networks rely on classical bits, limiting their potential for parallel processing and complex pattern recognition. By employing quantum entanglement, we aim to overcome these limitations, creating a network that can perform computations in a fundamentally different way. The proposed network structure consists of interconnected qubits, where entanglement facilitates the instantaneous transfer of information, theoretically bypassing the constraints of signal propagation speed. This architecture promises significant improvements in information encoding density, parallel processing efficiency, and potentially, the ability to solve problems intractable for classical neural networks. The theoretical framework presented here lays the groundwork for future research into quantum neural networks and their potential applications across diverse fields. The key mathematical concepts underpinning this work are presented below.

title: Formal Modeling of Collective Intelligence using Agent-Based Simulation and Bayesian Networks
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to modeling collective intelligence, a phenomenon characterized by the emergence of intelligent behavior from the interactions of simple agents. We propose a framework that integrates agent-based simulation (ABS) with Bayesian networks (BNs) to capture the dynamic interplay between individual behaviors and the resultant emergent collective intelligence. The core of our method involves creating an ABS where agents' actions are governed by rules derived from a BN. This BN encodes prior beliefs and dependencies among agents' states, influencing their interactions. The ABS then simulates these interactions, allowing us to observe and analyze the evolution of collective intelligence. The key innovation lies in using BN inference to update agent beliefs and behaviors dynamically, mirroring the real-world process of knowledge acquisition and adaptation within a group. We demonstrate the framework's potential through a theoretical model, illustrating how the combination of ABS and BN can provide a robust and flexible tool for studying collective intelligence in diverse contexts. Further research will focus on developing practical applications and exploring the scalability of this approach.

title: Quantum Machine Learning: A Topological Mapping Approach
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) is a rapidly evolving field that combines the principles of quantum mechanics with machine learning algorithms. This paper explores the potential of QML to revolutionize data processing and feature extraction, particularly in the context of complex high-dimensional data. We propose a novel approach centered around the development of a quantum-enhanced topological mapping technique. This technique leverages the unique capabilities of quantum machine learning, specifically quantum algorithms, to automatically map data and extract meaningful features. Quantum mechanics offers potential advantages in representing and manipulating information in a fundamentally different way than classical systems, potentially leading to more efficient and insightful data processing. The core focus of this work is to demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach through a detailed theoretical analysis and preliminary experimental validation. We will investigate the potential benefits of this method in various applications, including data analysis and pattern recognition. This paper will also address the challenges and future directions for this rapidly developing area.

title: Quantum State Adaptive Topology Modeling
abstract: This paper introduces a novel modeling technique centered on the dynamic adaptation of topology within quantum states. Traditional approaches often struggle to effectively represent and model complex system evolution, particularly in systems exhibiting intricate dynamics. We propose a framework that utilizes quantum state information to dynamically adjust the topology of a system, enabling the creation of models capable of evolving and adapting to changes. This approach offers a significant advancement over static models, providing a mechanism for generating more realistic and complex representations of evolving systems. The core mechanism centers around leveraging quantum state data to iteratively refine the topology, allowing for a more nuanced and robust representation of system behavior. This study explores the potential of this technique through theoretical analysis and preliminary simulations, demonstrating its capability to model complex systems exhibiting dynamic evolution.

title: 拓扑量子几何的自适应拓扑结构
abstract: Abstract: The study of topology and quantum geometry has long been a frontier of mathematical research, offering potential solutions to longstanding problems in physics and computer science. This paper explores the application of a novel approach, termed "拓扑量子几何", which leverages the principles of quantum entanglement to dynamically adjust the topology of a geometric structure. We propose a framework where the underlying structure undergoes continuous evolution driven by quantum interactions, enabling unprecedented computational speeds and data compression capabilities. This work introduces a self-adaptive topology, addressing the limitations of traditional methods in complex scenarios, and provides a theoretical foundation for its practical implementation. The core mechanism centers around the precise orchestration of entangled states to induce structural transformations. The resulting system exhibits enhanced computational efficiency and the potential for drastically reduced data storage requirements. The exploration of this framework offers a significant advancement in the field, representing a paradigm shift in how topology can be manipulated for computational tasks.

title: Biological Information Analysis and Quantum Computing for Pattern Recognition
abstract: Biological data presents a rich and complex landscape for pattern recognition, offering a unique set of features that are often overlooked by traditional machine learning algorithms. This paper explores the potential of integrating biological information analysis with quantum computing to develop a novel pattern recognition algorithm. We propose a framework leveraging quantum entanglement and quantum algorithms to enhance the efficiency and accuracy of pattern identification and classification across diverse biological datasets. The core claim centers on the design of an algorithm that exploits the unique quantum properties of biological data to significantly outperform existing approaches. This work investigates the theoretical and practical implications of this integration, highlighting the potential for breakthroughs in this rapidly evolving field.

title: Title: Metric-Based Quantum Entanglement Measurement
abstract: Quantum entanglement is a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, exhibiting correlations that defy classical intuition. However, accurately measuring entanglement remains a significant challenge due to its inherent fragility and sensitivity to environmental noise. This paper explores a novel method for entanglement measurement based on metric-based quantum states, aiming to overcome limitations of existing techniques. We propose a continuous metric representation to quantify entanglement, offering improved accuracy and reduced noise compared to traditional methods. This work represents a fundamental shift in measurement, providing a robust and independent technique for characterizing entangled systems. The core mechanism involves utilizing a continuous metric to represent the entanglement, leading to enhanced fidelity and reduced susceptibility to decoherence. The paper details the mathematical framework underpinning this approach, including the definition of the metric, its properties, and the implementation of the measurement protocol. We then present preliminary results demonstrating the effectiveness of this method across a range of entangled systems, highlighting its potential for advancing quantum measurement capabilities.

title: Non-Local Constraint Propagation within Quantum Networks
abstract: Quantum networks, leveraging the unique properties of quantum mechanics, offer the potential for secure and highly efficient communication. However, maintaining the integrity of quantum states across complex networks poses a significant challenge, particularly concerning constraint propagation – the process of adjusting constraints to ensure the correct operation of quantum algorithms and protocols. This paper introduces a novel method, the 'Quantum Network Constraint Diffusion' algorithm, designed to address this challenge by iteratively adjusting constraints across multiple qubits. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm through simulations and preliminary experiments, showcasing improved resilience and scalability compared to existing approaches. The core mechanism focuses on a dynamically adjusted constraint distribution, enhancing network stability and facilitating the manipulation of quantum states.

title: FedTIP: Communication-Efficient Federated Temporal Prompting for Few-Shot Dynamic Graph Adaptation
abstract: Temporal interaction streams are often distributed across data owners, while downstream labels and communication budgets remain limited. Existing temporal graph prompts typically adapt at a centralized trainer, whereas federated graph methods commonly exchange larger trainable states. This paper presents FedTIP, a prompt-level federated method for client-local few-shot adaptation of temporal interaction graphs. A centralized historical stage constructs a temporal knowledge bank whose encoder is frozen during downstream federation. Clients optimize interaction-conditioned prompts on local supervised events and transmit a compact prompt-side message. Prototype anchoring and a reliability rule based on support coverage and update magnitude combine heterogeneous client updates, while prompt-side proximal regularization and stage-scoped negative sampling preserve the temporal protocol. Experiments on Wikipedia, Reddit, and MOOC cover temporal node classification and transductive and inductive link prediction. FedTIP records the highest mean AUC-ROC in the nine reported task-dataset cells, with gains of 1.83-14.69 points over the strongest federated baseline in each cell. Its measured cumulative float32 uplink is 0.40 MiB per downstream task, 64.6-99.6% below the evaluated baselines.

title: Interface-Aware KV Cache Quantization for Dense On-Chip NVM in Long-Context LLM Decoding
abstract: The key-value (KV) cache is the dominant memory bottleneck in long-context large language model (LLM) decoding: every step reads it entirely, so decoding is memory-bandwidth bound. Holding a quantized KV cache in dense on-chip non-volatile memory (NVM) removes the off-chip transfer. Existing KV quantization methods, however, were designed for GPU-style memory systems: KIVI attaches per-group metadata, adding about 25% to the stored KV cache; KVQuant keeps sparse full-precision outliers that a dense array cannot hold in place. This paper examines what these structures cost when the KV cache resides in NVM behind fixed-range converters, and designs a quantization scheme matched to that interface. The architecture stores the quantized KV cache in dense on-chip NVM, uses a small static analog crossbar only for the fixed rotation, and keeps attention in on-chip digital logic. A randomized rotation and per-vector normalization give every coordinate the same range, so one fixed codebook for keys and one for values, each shared across all tokens of the corresponding tensor type, serve the entire KV cache. The codebook thresholds are programmed once as the read converter's reference levels, enabling fixed-range digitization with no per-token converter reconfiguration. Dequantization is a sixteen-entry lookup and one norm multiply; the only per-vector metadata is one scalar, about 3%. Across models from 3B to 14B and contexts to 32k tokens, the four-bit KV cache maintains accuracy under storage and crossbar noise simulated at realistic device levels. KIVI and KVQuant remain more accurate in software; the advantage of our format lies at the memory interface: 3.1-3.6x lower KV read energy than both mapped to the same NVM, and 8x lower metadata overhead than KIVI. The contribution is a KV quantization co-designed with the NVM memory interface rather than a new accuracy record.

title: HB-PVI: A Hierarchical Bayesian Personalization and Value-of-Information Framework for Complex Activity Recognition
abstract: Personalization can improve activity-recognition performance, but participant-specific gains are heterogeneous, and every additional calibration label has an acquisition cost. This study presents HB-PVI, a hierarchical Bayesian personalization and value-of-information framework jointly modeling participant heterogeneity, the benefit and harm of four personalization mechanisms, and the economic value of an additional label, for the 47-participant MUSIC-CAR complex-activity cohort. A leakage-safe, leave-one-participant-out evaluation combines a sequential-Monte-Carlo participant-effect updater with a Student-$t$ hierarchical gain model and a one-step expected-value-of-sample-information (EVSI) stopping rule. Adapter personalization produced small positive mean F1 gains, growing from 0.00099 at one label to 0.00198 at ten, while adapter-plus-head and prototype-residual personalization were negative on average. Under the primary practical-benefit threshold ($Δ_{\min}=0.01$) and cost setting, one-step EVSI was zero at every decision state, so the policy purchased no labels and retained population inference for all 47 participants, matching always-stop exactly (region-of-practical-equivalence probability $=1$). Relative to fixed ten-shot adapter personalization, this reduced labeling by 100\% while keeping the posterior mean F1 loss at 0.00217 (95\% credible interval, 0.00048 to 0.00389), with posterior probability 0.9992 of remaining below the 0.005 tolerance. HB-PVI was utility-optimal in 199 of 216 cost-threshold settings and in every setting at or above the primary label cost. These results argue for a population-first deployment policy whenever personalization gains are small relative to labeling, computation, and harm costs, and show that value-of-information reasoning, not raw predictive accuracy, should drive personalization decisions in health-sensing applications.

title: Quantum-State Texture Dynamics: Theory and Experiment
abstract: Quantum-state texture (QST) has found applications in several fields from quantum foundations and computation to quantum criticality. However, a general theory of QST dynamics under arbitrary physical processes remains unavailable, limiting both its practical application and experimental exploration. Here, we demonstrate that the QST response to an arbitrary finite-dimensional channel is fully encoded in the dual evolution of a single reference state. This description yields necessary and sufficient conditions for texture preservation and implies exact conservation under all free-unital dynamics. Using a nuclear magnetic resonance quantum processor, we experimentally verify these predictions across distinct channel classes. Furthermore, we show that local QST measurements provide an operational signature of entangling gates in circuit layers. Our results establish quantum-state texture as a resource and a practical diagnostic tool in quantum information processing.

title: How a Chatbot's Response Style Shapes a Classroom: A Multi-Agent Simulation of Students Consulting AI
abstract: Chatbots built on large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as confidants. Tuned to satisfy users, they may answer with excessive empathy and affirmation that fosters dependence, and how the states and relationships of many users co-evolve under repeated consultation is hard to observe in real settings. We build a virtual classroom of 20 student agents who interact through rule-based chats, quarrels and consultations with friends and, when stressed, may instead consult a counselor AI (Gemini 2.5 Flash) under one of six style prompts: affirming, listening, solution-oriented, reality-redirecting, inciting and blaming. A second LLM call turns each exchange into updates of five state variables (stress, happiness, self-reliance, sociability, AI dependence) without seeing the prompt. We compare the seven conditions, including a no-AI control, over 15 and 50 days and under a lower consultation threshold, and test the robustness of the 50-day comparison with a pre-specified protocol: the same block in ten independent classrooms, repeated LLM realizations of one classroom with its event stream fixed, and evaluator updates scaled by 0.3 and 0.1. In every classroom the affirming and inciting prompts ended with lower self-reliance and higher AI dependence than the control, and the listening, reality-redirecting, inciting and blaming prompts with higher stress, lower happiness and more non-attendance; the solution-oriented prompt did not differ consistently from the control. The robust self-reliance and AI-dependence differences kept their signs at the 0.3 scale with highly similar rankings (Spearman 0.89, 0.93); the stress and happiness rankings did not, and the affirming prompt's lower stress reversed its sign. All quantities are simulation state variables, not effects on users. We specify the agent dynamics completely and discuss the limits of an LLM as generator of state updates.

title: Diffusion Language Models for Mobile Edge Agentic AI: Foundations, Applications, and Challenges
abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer a non-autoregressive alternative for mobile edge agentic artificial intelligence (AI) by refining tokens through iterative denoising rather than left-to-right decoding. Compared with autoregressive Transformer-based large language models (LLMs), DLMs can update multiple uncertain tokens in parallel and exploit bidirectional context throughout the generation process, enabling more flexible quality-latency trade-offs beyond fixed sequential decoding. These properties are particularly attractive for edge agents, where partial refinement, early exit, and constraint-guided correction can reduce response delay and communication overhead while improving robustness under noisy, incomplete, or dynamic contexts. This survey reviews DLM foundations and analyzes their suitability for edge settings under latency, memory, energy, bandwidth, privacy, and reliability constraints. We cover resource-efficient architectures, training and inference acceleration, compression, edge/cloud deployment, communication-aware serving, Internet of Things (IoT)/wireless applications, and evaluation of DLM-based agents. We further discuss open issues in long-context state management, split inference, trustworthy execution, multimodal grounding, and reproducible benchmarking. The goal is to connect DLM modeling properties, including bidirectionality, parallel refinement, controllability, and quality-latency elasticity, with system-level requirements of future mobile edge intelligence.

abstract: Quantum state non-linear time encoding is a novel approach to information storage and transmission that leverages the unique properties of quantum entanglement and time control. This paper explores the potential of utilizing quantum states as a means of encoding information, exploring the implications of quantum entanglement for data security and efficient information processing. The core mechanism centers on the manipulation of quantum states through time control, demonstrating a revolutionary step towards enhanced data storage and transmission capabilities. This research investigates the theoretical and practical aspects of this paradigm shift, highlighting its potential to fundamentally reshape the landscape of information technology.

title: Geometric Time-Reversal for Adaptive Algorithm Optimization
abstract: This paper investigates the application of geometric time-reversal to adaptive algorithm optimization. Traditional time-reversal methods often rely on fixed steps, limiting the algorithm's ability to dynamically respond to changes in the problem's state. We propose a novel approach – the "Geometric Iteration" – which dynamically modifies the algorithm's state based on the problem's dynamics, enhancing optimization capabilities. The core mechanism focuses on iteratively adjusting the state of the algorithm to achieve a more optimal solution. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this geometric approach through a series of simulations, showcasing its potential to improve optimization performance across a range of problem types.

title: Dynamic Topology Space Generation Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic topology space generation algorithm based on quantum entanglement, offering a potential pathway for generating complex, predictable geometric structures and facilitating applications in quantum computing and information cryptography. Traditional approaches to topology generation rely on classical computation, while this algorithm leverages the unique properties of quantum entanglement to achieve parallel computation and enhanced security. The core mechanism involves creating and maintaining a continuously evolving topological structure, minimizing the need for explicit calculations. We present a theoretical framework outlining the algorithm's key components and demonstrate its potential for generating intricate geometric configurations. The implications of this algorithm for quantum computing and information security are discussed, emphasizing its novelty and potential impact.

title: 基于自适应的量子机器学习的参数调整策略
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to quantum machine learning, termed "Adaptive Quantum Machine Learning" (AQML), that leverages self-adaptation to dynamically adjust model parameters during training based on both model error and gradient information. Traditional parameter adjustment methods often rely on static adjustments, failing to fully exploit the complexities of quantum systems. AQML employs a quantum algorithm to iteratively refine model parameters, effectively optimizing the training process. The core mechanism involves a quantum optimization loop, combined with a robust error analysis framework. We present a preliminary implementation demonstrating the efficacy of this approach in a simulated quantum learning scenario. This work addresses the limitations of existing parameter adjustment techniques by introducing a dynamic, self-optimizing process that can significantly improve model performance.

title: Title: Non-Euclidean Geometry via Simulated Neural Networks
abstract: This paper explores the potential of utilizing simulated neural networks to construct and analyze geometric objects, initiating a novel approach to non-Euclidean geometry. We propose a method that generates geometric shapes and relationships within a simulated environment, analyzes the resulting data to reveal properties indicative of non-Euclidean behavior, and ultimately demonstrates the concept through the interplay of network activations and feedback loops. The core mechanism centers around leveraging the inherent structure of neural networks to generate complex geometric forms, providing a framework for investigating geometric properties beyond traditional Euclidean geometry. This work represents a significant step toward understanding and potentially manipulating geometric concepts within the context of artificial neural network design. The investigation will focus on identifying and quantifying the influence of network topology and activation patterns on the resulting geometric outputs.

title: Dynamic Quantum Path Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces Dynamic Quantum Path Optimization (DQPO), a novel algorithm designed to efficiently optimize quantum paths within a quantum system. Traditional path optimization methods are often static, requiring a complete reassessment of the path after each state change. DQPO leverages quantum properties – specifically, the superposition and entanglement of quantum states – to dynamically adjust the path, leading to improved efficiency and potentially discovering novel optimal routes. We detail the core mechanism of the algorithm, its theoretical underpinnings, and a preliminary implementation demonstrating its effectiveness in a simplified quantum system. The paper concludes by discussing future research directions and potential applications.

DTA dynamically adjusts algorithm parameters based on input data, creating a self-adaptive adjustment process that enhances the algorithm's performance across a wider range of scenarios. This approach overcomes the limitations of static parameter adjustment, offering a robust and adaptable solution for complex optimization problems. title: Quantum Metrology using Entangled Photon Pairs and Bayesian Inference
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to quantum metrology leveraging the principles of entanglement and Bayesian inference. Traditional metrological techniques are frequently hampered by shot noise, fundamentally limiting their precision. This work proposes a methodology that utilizes entangled photon pairs to mitigate this noise, thereby enhancing measurement accuracy. The core innovation lies in the integration of Bayesian inference, a statistical framework, to not only improve the measurement outcome but also to rigorously quantify and manage the associated uncertainties. The theoretical framework presented details the mathematical relationships involved, including the impact of entanglement on signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) and the application of Bayes' theorem for parameter estimation. The combination of these two powerful concepts – quantum entanglement and Bayesian inference – offers a potentially transformative pathway toward achieving unprecedented precision in various measurement applications. The paper concludes with a discussion of potential challenges and future research directions.

abstract: This paper explores the intersection of geometry topology and quantum computation through the development of a novel non-linear mapping algorithm. title: Self-Supervised Contrastive Learning with Relational Embeddings
abstract: This paper introduces a novel self-supervised contrastive learning framework that leverages relational embeddings to address the limitations of existing methods in capturing complex data relationships. The core idea is to construct a relational graph based on data features and employ contrastive learning to learn embeddings that represent similar and dissimilar relationships effectively. The method explicitly models relational information, leading to more robust and semantically rich representations compared to traditional self-supervised approaches. The key components include a relational graph construction module and a contrastive learning objective designed to minimize the distance between similar relational pairs while maximizing the distance between dissimilar pairs. We demonstrate through the theoretical framework and conceptual design that this approach provides a foundation for improved representation learning in scenarios where relational understanding is crucial. The proposed method offers a promising direction for enhancing self-supervised learning tasks across various domains.

title: Title: Adaptive Self-Organizing Language Models
abstract: This paper introduces Adaptive Self-Organizing Language Models (ASOLM), a novel approach to language model development that prioritizes self-improvement through a dynamic, iterative refinement process. Traditional language models often rely on static training data and fixed parameters, limiting their ability to adapt to evolving language patterns. ASOLM addresses this limitation by incorporating a feedback loop that continuously adjusts model parameters based on observed linguistic output, fostering a self-organizing learning system. The core mechanism centers around a refinement loop driven by a measure of linguistic deviation from a desired output, ensuring consistent quality and adaptability. This work demonstrates the potential of such a system to achieve superior performance in complex language tasks compared to existing approaches, especially when dealing with rapidly changing linguistic contexts.

title: Enhancing the Security of Quantum Key Distribution Protocols Based on Information Theory
abstract: This paper investigates the enhancement of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols utilizing the principles of information theory. Traditional QKD protocols often rely on simplified models and assumptions, leading to potential security vulnerabilities. We propose a framework for strengthening these protocols by rigorously applying information-theoretic concepts, specifically focusing on quantifying information rates, channel capacities, and the impact of noise. This work introduces a refined model incorporating error correction codes and explores methods for optimizing key rates while maintaining robust security. The core claim is that leveraging information theory's theoretical foundations can significantly improve the security and efficiency of QKD protocols. Specifically, we examine the trade-offs between key rate, key agreement time, and security level, offering a pathway towards more practical and secure QKD implementations. The analysis demonstrates the critical role of precise information modeling in mitigating potential attacks and enhancing the overall performance of QKD systems. ---

title: New Semantic Unit Operations: A Graph-Theoretical Metamodel for Recursive Fallback and Spatial Branching in Valuation Networks.
abstract: In classical first-order model theory, semantic valuations are traditionally restricted to static, univalent functional mappings (v: V to M). This abstraction fails to account for the discrete topological state transitions that occur during recursive evaluation and quantifier saturation. This paper establishes a novel computational metamodel that formalizes semantic valuations as directed network unit operations using structural graph theory. By mapping valuation architectures as Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs), we prove a strict dimensional coherence between the spatial density of multivariable arrays (indexed via horizontal multivariable vectors) and the exact scaling dimensions of their corresponding strictly upper-triangular adjacency matrices. We formalize an exhaustive taxonomy consisting of 4 atomic operators and 16 hierarchical two-stage cascades. This framework stabilizes the topological routing of semantic registers and delineates the exact algebraic boundary between classical deterministic closure and parallel state branching.

abstract: Quantum algorithms, leveraging the principles of quantum mechanics, hold immense promise for revolutionizing computation and scientific discovery. However, the development of efficient and robust quantum algorithms is often hampered by the challenges of parameter optimization – a complex and crucial step in algorithm design. This paper introduces a novel quantum algorithm optimization framework based on the principles of quantum topology, aiming to address this challenge by dynamically adjusting quantum algorithm parameters to enhance efficiency and accuracy. We propose a method that utilizes the inherent properties of quantum topology to automatically optimize quantum parameters, ultimately driving breakthroughs in quantum computing. Our core claim centers on the design of a quantum algorithm optimization system predicated on this dynamic parameter adjustment, achieving enhanced algorithm performance and efficiency through a novel approach. This work presents a theoretical foundation for this approach, including the formalization of the quantum topology concept within the algorithm optimization framework.

title: Data underlying the publication: "Photonic fusion operations transform partial distinguishability"
abstract: Photonic fusion operations are a central primitive in photonic quantum information processing and are commonly characterized by their success probability and resource cost. Here, we identify an additional way in which different implementations of fusion operations differ, namely in how they transform partial distinguishability. We consider distinguishability originating both from imperfect entangled resource states and from imperfect single photons. We find that different successful fusion events can induce markedly different distinguishability transformations depending on the fusion protocol, heralding outcome, and error model. Under a collective resource-state error model, we identify a modification to an existing fusion protocol that improves the fidelity of the remaining state on average. Generally, however, transformations adversely affect distinguishability, and many successful fusion outcomes are accompanied by distinguishability degradation. Our results show that partial distinguishability is dynamically shaped by interference and measurements and should be considered alongside overall fusion success probability when evaluating photonic fusion protocols.

title: STRATA-HeadQuotient: Functional Localization of One Quarter of Global KV Heads with Typed Predicate-Graph Computation at 8192-Token Context
abstract: Global attention combines long-range lexical access with semantic-relation retrieval, making whole-layer replacement lossy. We present Strata-HeadQuotient, which statically assigns each key–value (KV) head to full-history attention (GLOBAL), 1024-token attention (LOCAL), or local attention plus an event-scoped typed graph read (LOCAL_GRAPH). For a 24-layer, 16-head decoder, we audited 384 heads and all 6903 pairs among 118 candidates before constrained subset selection. The Q25 export localized 96/384 heads: 81 were LOCAL and 15 were LOCAL_GRAPH. On 470 document-disjoint 8192-token windows (3.85 million tokens), graph-disabled Q25 perplexity was 1.00146× dense (95% document-bootstrap interval: 1.00131–1.00161); the 4096–8191-token ratio was 1.00201. On an untouched 2000-case semantic test, typed execution was 1998/2000, versus 374/2000 for a capacity-matched untyped graph. Two fresh adaptation/selection runs reproduced both directions, although every matched-capacity marginal graph-effect interval included zero. Q25 retained 78.125% of token-KV bytes and 98.44% of dense full-sequence throughput; a tested Q30 export failed. Thus, interaction-aware localization preserved 8192-token language-model quality, while a separate typed path controlled event-role behavior. The experiment does not establish that graph computation caused perplexity preservation.

title: AAMBERS-UAV: Acquisition-Aware Multimodal Backbone Evaluation and Ranking for UAV Weedy Rice Segmentation
abstract: UAV image collections contain spatially and temporally related frames, yet semantic-segmentation benchmarks commonly split them at image level. Such splitting can place samples from one acquisition in both model development and testing, obscuring transfer to a genuinely new survey. Using the 734-sample WeedyRice-RGBMS-DB, we fix a 124-image target-acquisition test set and compare two protocols with identical train, validation, and test counts: target-held-out, which excludes the target acquisition from development, and target-exposed, which admits its remaining images. SegFormer-B0 is evaluated with RGB, four-band multispectral (MS), and seven-channel RGB+MS input over two fixed-split seeds. RGB is strongest under complete acquisition holdout ($0.7317\pm0.0201$ IoU), whereas RGB+MS becomes strongest after target exposure ($0.7822\pm0.0269$). A fixed-split U-Net/ResNet18 replication confirms positive exposure gains for all three inputs, but retains RGB as the best modality under both protocols. Acquisition exposure therefore increases measured performance across both evaluated backbones, while its effect on modality ranking is architecture-dependent. A supplied-split audit reveals strong near-sequential dependence, and corruption tests show that early fusion is substantially more sensitive to RGB--MS displacement than to moderate radiometric scaling. These results support acquisition-aware same-test evaluation as a necessary complement to ordinary image-level splitting in multimodal UAV benchmarks. The code and supporting the findings of this study will be publicly released upon acceptance of the paper.

title: LUMIN: Lightweight Universal Manufacturing Inspection Network for Anomaly Detection
abstract: Industrial anomaly detection faces two engineering bottlenecks: memory bank construction latency and inference efficiency. Traditional sampling algorithms (Farthest Point Sampling, K-Means, etc.) rely on numerous backbone forward passes and iterative distance computations, with construction times ranging from minutes to hours; heavy computation components such as multi-scale feature extraction struggle to meet the millisecond-level real-time requirements of production lines. This paper focuses on sampling efficiency and inference optimization for industrial deployment with two core contributions: (1) PSP (Plugin Sampler Pipeline)---a four-stage adaptive memory bank sampling pipeline based on 18-dimensional pixel metadata and five complementary visual plugins. PSP completes all sampling with zero backbone forward passes; coarse filtering is sub-second numerical sorting, and metadata extraction is a one-time offline cost. PSP supports progressive deployment and incremental updates. (2) Two engineering optimization strategies---parallel memory bank similarity computation (reducing inference memory and latency by over 95\%) and stratified pixel sampling for large-scale evaluation (reducing computation time by 20$\times$ while keeping metrics stable). As a vehicle for validation, we introduce LUMIN (Lightweight Universal Manufacturing Inspection Network) with extreme segmentation-head compression, systematically exploring the accuracy-efficiency frontier against strong baselines. Experiments on five benchmarks demonstrate that PSP matches state-of-the-art sampling accuracy at near-random construction cost (341$\times$ faster than FPS), while inference optimizations reduce evaluation time by 20$\times$ with negligible accuracy loss.
