title: Symmetry Groups of the Platonic Solid POVMs: Binary Polyhedral Groups as Quantum Circuits
abstract: We study the symmetry groups of the Platonic solid POVMs: the binary polyhedral groups 2T, 2O, and 2I, exact unitary 2-, 3-, and 5-designs. A unified treatment, bringing together mathematical construction, quantum circuits, and cost, is missing. We provide it, in the single-qubit setting, via two complementary constructions and a compilation, implemented with symbolic computation. The result is an atlas of all 192 group elements, fully reproducible from accompanying code, its gate sequences, none deeper than four, doubling as POVM rotation circuits. Once anchored to the Pauli group, 2T and 2O are entirely Clifford, while the binary icosahedral group 2I requires at most one non-Clifford gate per element—the golden gate Φ. As a double-coset decomposition, 2I = 2T ⊔ 2T Φ 2T. We prove that only the octahedral POVM admits exact implementation over our gate sets (Clifford+T among them), and never deterministically; in our orientation, the other four point at magic states. We consider the POVMs in classical shadow estimation, where an inexact implementation is paid for in estimator variance; scalability keeps us to local shadows, a per-qubit factorized regime. We compare two randomized implementations: both support robust shadow estimation, but calibrate different scalars; calibration must match protocol. Every Platonic solid POVM has a Naimark dilation circuit, though never an exact one, and a prepended draw from 2T, the least group that suffices, twirls measurement-side noise to exactly depolarizing (a fixed approximation costs variance, never bias). Only the antipodal solids decompose into projective measurements, which excludes the tetrahedral SIC. There, one drawn rotation must both realize the POVM and twirl the noise: among groups, granted by 2T for all but the dodecahedron, which requires 2I.

title: Quantum Topology: An Intrinsic Information Encoding and Transfer Method
abstract: Quantum topology, a fascinating field of physics, offers the potential for novel information encoding and transmission methods. This paper explores the application of quantum topology to design a secure and efficient information transfer protocol. We propose a method leveraging the unique properties of quantum topology, specifically the formation of topological defects and the interplay of quantum entanglement, to achieve information security and enhanced transmission speeds. This research focuses on a novel approach that utilizes the inherent structure of quantum systems to create a robust and adaptable system for secure communication. The core mechanism involves exploiting topological properties to circumvent traditional cryptographic vulnerabilities. The paper details the theoretical underpinnings, proposes a practical implementation framework, and discusses the potential implications for future quantum information security.

title: 基于量子纠缠的复杂计算模型
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum entanglement as a novel computational paradigm to address the limitations of traditional computing models. We propose a new computational model predicated on the dynamic behavior of entangled quantum states, aiming to achieve precise modeling and simulation of complex systems. The core mechanism focuses on establishing a quantum entanglement-based dynamic simulation model, leveraging the inherent non-linear properties of entanglement to facilitate accurate computations. The research investigates the advantages of this approach, particularly the potential for automated parameter adjustment and reduced computational complexity compared to traditional methods. The paper details the theoretical framework underpinning this model and presents preliminary results demonstrating the feasibility of this approach in simulating specific complex systems.

title: DW-FMAL Wireless Interference Dataset
abstract: This dataset contains 800,000 simulated I/Q samples for cross-domain wireless interference recognition under domain shifts caused by transmitter devices, propagation channels, and interference-to-noise ratios. It covers 16 interference classes over a complete grid of 5 devices, 5 channel conditions, and 5 INR values, forming 125 domains. Each sample contains 512 complex-baseband sampling points represented by two float32 I/Q channels. The dataset supports the associated paper Cross-domain wireless interference recognition via dynamically weighted adversarial learning.

title: 自组织拓扑结构的量子计算控制
abstract: Quantum computing offers the potential for unprecedented computational power, but maintaining qubit coherence and control remains a significant challenge. This paper explores the application of self-organized topological structures to quantum computation, proposing a novel control scheme that leverages these structures for enhanced stability and dynamic manipulation. We investigate the design of a control protocol centered around the formation and manipulation of specific topological defects, aiming to achieve robust quantum states. The core mechanism involves utilizing the inherent properties of these structures to dynamically adjust qubit states, mitigating decoherence and facilitating precise control. The research focuses on establishing a stable, self-organized quantum state, demonstrating a significant improvement in qubit coherence compared to traditional control strategies. This work represents a fundamental advancement in quantum control methodology, with potential implications for the scalability and reliability of quantum systems.

title: 基于多尺度学习的神经网络的动态拓扑映射
abstract: This paper introduces a novel neural network architecture, termed "Dynamic Topology Mapping Network" (DTMN), that leverages a multi-scale learning approach to effectively map and transform topological structures across different scales. The DTMN employs a recurrent neural network (RNN) core coupled with a hierarchical feature extraction mechanism, enabling it to learn intricate relationships within complex datasets. We explore the benefits of this architecture, particularly its capacity to generalize better to unseen data, by focusing on the dynamic representation of topological relationships. The paper details the design of the DTMN, the training process, and results demonstrating its superior performance in a variety of topological mapping tasks. The core claim is that the DTMN achieves significantly improved generalization compared to traditional network architectures through the implementation of dynamic topology mapping. We present experimental results showcasing the enhanced performance of the DTMN across diverse datasets, highlighting its effectiveness in representing and manipulating topological changes. Finally, we discuss the limitations of the current approach and suggest directions for future research.

title: Reproducibility Record for "Budgeting cost is reproducible, comparing it is not: cross-execution stability of resource-aware stopping in automated machine learning"
abstract: This record supports an interventional study of when a hyperparameter-search stopping rule reproduces its own decision. The same search was executed twice at each of ten seeds on CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18 under a pre-registered protocol, and thirteen stopping policies observed identical trial sequences in each execution. It contains the frozen pre-registration, the run receipts and candidate logs for all 32 campaign cells, the policy panel and both decision paths, the analysis that emits the single results file from which every number in the article is drawn, the figure scripts, the two pre-campaign live-versus-replay equivalence logs, a map from each reported table and figure to its source files, and the provenance gate that checks the article against the results file. One observation cell was contaminated by concurrent activity on the measurement machine and is retained rather than removed; every quantity is reported over both the full and the reduced population. The record also preserves the pre-registered mechanism test that failed and the exploratory arm, neither of which supports the authors' expectations. CIFAR-10 is not redistributed. Code and scripts are MIT licensed; derived evidence, documentation, tables and metadata are CC BY 4.0. Version 1.1.0 adds the replication campaign C2: 284 further cells across four arms (Adult at 12 seeds by 10 executions, PJM hourly load at 10 by 2, CIFAR-10 at 3 by 4, and Adult again on a quiet machine at 12 by 2), its analysis plan with predictions committed before the data, one results file per arm, two further figures, and the timestamped logs of every inspection made on the machine while a run was in progress and of the machine-state changes the analysis conditions on. Registered predictions are graded as written; anything marked exploratory was not in the plan.

title: SAEF: An Adaptive and Explainable Feedback System for Personalized Learning
abstract: Adaptive and explainable systems are two critical concepts in personalized learning that enhance the customized experience based on the adjusted content according to the individual learning of a learner. In this paper, we present a modular and interpretable architecture for the development of a System for Adaptive and Explainable Feedback, which is a potential solution for the above-mentioned issues in personalized learning environments. The adaptive feedback provided by the System for Adaptive and Explainable Feedback is in real time. Still, even more importantly, it is justified clearly and transparently so that both the learner and instructor understand the why behind the recommendations for action given by the system. It consists of modular technologies for data collection (word and phrase occurrence, time tracking), analysis (latency, process mining), feedback generation (adaptive after-action review), and result presentation, making a modular, flexible, and scalable system to suit many educational scenarios. To evaluate the system’s functional performance, the SAEF pipeline was applied to a dataset derived from the ASSISTments platform, a well-established educational dataset widely used in learning analytics research. On a cohort of 500 student profiles, the SAEF achieved an overall recommendation accuracy of 83.6%, a weighted F1-score of 82.9%, and a mean system response time of 42.1 ms, demonstrating both the internal computational consistency and efficiency of the adaptive pipeline. These results indicate strong agreement with score-derived difficulty categories and support the internal computational consistency of the recommendation pipeline as a proof-of-concept system, though they do not constitute independent evidence of instructional appropriateness. The SAEF is designed to support learner engagement, personalize learning pathways, and foster transparency in AI-driven educational environments; a full empirical evaluation involving real-world deployment is identified as the primary direction for future work. The perceived understandability, trustworthiness, and pedagogical usefulness of the SAEF’s explanations by learners and instructors represent a complementary dimension yet to be empirically explored. The SAEF’s architecture is designed with the explicit objective of supporting learner engagement and fostering transparency; however, these pedagogical benefits are architectural design goals rather than empirically demonstrated outcomes in the present study, which focuses exclusively on computational validation.

title: Boundary-Centered Explainability for Dialogue Topic Segmentation
abstract: Despite recent advances in dialogue topic segmentation, existing work provides limited evidence about why individual utterances are predicted as boundaries and how local explanations depend on the selection strategy and perturbation protocol. Using fixed checkpoints of 3LHSeg, a hierarchical dialogue topic segmentation model, we evaluate a boundary-centered framework that compares five local utterance-selection strategies through complementary perturbation diagnostics. The audit also examines configuration sensitivity and explanation stability and uses Random-Baseline Gain (RBG) as a diagnostic of relative local distinctiveness by contextualizing comprehensiveness against matched random subsets from the same local candidate window. Experiments on TIAGE, QMSum, and Friends show that Leave-One-Out ranks most favorably under the adopted perturbation-based diagnostics, although this result is protocol-specific. The diagnostics provide partially overlapping information and vary with the local configuration. Raw deletion area-under-the-curve values are consistently positively associated with initial boundary confidence, but a centered control substantially attenuates this association in most dataset–strategy combinations. Overall, explanation behavior, probability quality, confidence, stability, and boundary correctness should be treated as distinct dimensions, supporting multi-diagnostic and configuration-explicit auditing rather than reliance on a single explanation score.

title: HistoNav: AI-Based H&E Histopathology Predicts Disease-Specific Survival and Guides Adjuvant Chemotherapy Decisions in Stage II/IIIA Colorectal Cancer
abstract: Background: Stage II/IIIA colorectal cancer (CRC) patients have a relatively high 5-year overall survival rate after surgical resection alone, but more than 50% of patients receive adjuvant chemotherapy. This study investigates a technology that applies artificial intelligence (AI) to conventional histopathology images to identify patients at risk of recurrence. Methods: HistoNav, a novel AI deep-learning algorithm based on Vision Transformer, Graph Neural Networks and Convolutional Neural Networks was designed to analyse H&E-stained formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) samples (n = 2095) to stratify Stage II/IIIA CRC patients into low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups. Results: Data analysis revealed a 5-year disease-specific survival (DSS) of 93.2%, 84.3%, and 69.3% for low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups, respectively. The hazard ratio for the high versus low-risk group (HR = 4.611, 95% CI: 2.776–7.662; p < 0.000001) was statistically significant, demonstrating HistoNav’s potential to stratify patients based on recurrence risk. Conclusions: HistoNav can effectively identify CRC patients with good prognosis using the digital images of H&E-stained resection samples and will support clinical decisions around the use of adjuvant chemotherapy.

title: Confidence interval of a mean
abstract: Abstract This chapter establishes a smooth link to the previous section by discussing the calculation of the confidence interval of a mean, which requires learning how to exploit the t-distribution and calculate the t-statistic. We will learn: why a t-distribution can be approximated to a normal distribution when the sample size becomes large; how to properly define a custom Python function; and how to calculate the confidence interval of the standard deviation. The Pingouin package, which will be used in almost all chapters, is introduced. We also show how the bootstrapping approach, which generates a large number of pseudosamples by drawing random samples from the original data, creates a distribution that approximates the true population mean. This technique seems like magic, but has been widely documented by mathematicians and is increasingly used in statistics. Thanks to Python, it can be exploited efficiently and easily, and we can take advantage of its power in our own analyses.

title: Generative AI and Agentic Operations
abstract: Build, scale, and govern the next generation of autonomous AI agents The real AI revolution is not in the models themselves, but in their application to the messy, complex, and vital work of running a business. The real challenge is not “how does an agent work?” but “how do I manage a team of people and agent operations?” Generative AI and Agentic Operations: Reliable, Scalable, Safe Systems provides the missing blueprint for this transition. It offers a practical, operator-first guide to building and managing autonomous agents that don’t just replace rote tasks, but fundamentally augment and elevate human expertise. Central to this book is the Agentic Ops Lifecycle, a rigorous five-phase framework designed to take you from a fragile prototype to a resilient, production-grade system. Moving beyond traditional MLOps, this guide breaks down the “black box” of LLM reasoning and provides a structured approach to defining, building, evaluating, productionizing, and maintaining a non-deterministic digital workforce. The book also provides: Tactics for process re-engineering, showing how to consolidate complex workflows and unlock massive operational scale using agentic tools and reasoning loops. Proven strategies for managing a blended “Human+Agent” workforce, shifting human operators from task execution to system supervision and exception handling. A modernized approach to operational metrics and scorecards, moving beyond traditional handle times to measure holistic system quality, cost, and automation rates. Essential frameworks for navigating the ethical and regulatory “grey areas” of AI, including mitigating systemic bias, halting “runaway agents,” and building robust security guardrails. Practical insights and real-world case studies drawn from the front lines of transforming complex, large-scale data operations at Google Maps. Written for the operations leaders, managers, and team leads tasked with integrating AI into their workflows, this book is also essential reading for the product managers and engineers designing these systems. It delivers the strategic vision and the operational depth needed to successfully navigate the Agentic Age.

title: Message Passing Techniques in Graph‐Based Learning
abstract: The graph data structure consists of nodes and its connecting edges. Graph establishes relationship between nodes and exploits the dependencies among. The graphs enable various applications of the algorithm which enhances the relationship between the nodes in such a way that they can be used for optimization, improve user experience, and decision making. Graph-based learning is a machine learning paradigm based on graphical data that analyses and represents them by exploring hidden patterns. These new insights can be applied in various fields such as knowledge graphs, biological systems, recommender systems, molecular structures, network analysis, fraud detection, and information retrieval systems. Deeper understanding of data through the lens of graphical structures can provide power to organizations to make data-driven decisions. In the field of deep learning with graph data, GNNs (Graph Neural Networks) are modeled specially to work with graph data structures. They are successful, dominant, and fast-growing paradigms in artificial neural networks and deep learning. To learn complex relationships and exploit hidden patterns among nodes in a graph, GNN uses message passing technique. In this technique the representations of nodes are updated by exchanging information between them. This updated information is propagated throughout the graph. Each node aggregates data from neighboring nodes iteratively forming new relationships. This process helps in graph related tasks such as node classification, link prediction, and graph representation learning. The goal of this chapter is to provide a synthesis and overview of message passing technique in graph-based learning.

title: A complete characterization of sequential testability and change detectability in i.i.d. models
abstract: We give a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of power-one sequential tests in an i.i.d. composite testing problem. A level-\(α\) test with power one against every alternative exists if and only if the alternatives are separated from the null by a countable family of finite-block events. We provide other equivalent conditions using randomized fixed-sample tests, bounded finite-block scores, e-processes, reduced-filtration test supermartingales, and a countable cover whose finite-block weak-$*$ closed convex hulls are positively separated in total variation. As a bonus, the constructive proof yields tests have pointwise expected sample size \(O_Q(\log(1/α))\). Exactly the same conditions also characterize i.i.d.\ change detectability under optional-horizon average-run-length control: for every \(η>0\), they are equivalent to an alarm family \((T_γ)_{γ\ge1}\) satisfying \(\Prob_{P^\infty}(T_γ\leσ)\le \E_{P^\infty}σ/γ\) for every null law and every stopping time \(σ\). In fact, when these conditions hold, we can construct a single e-detector such that every null-law average run length lies between \(γ\) and \((1+η)γ+1\), and having robust Lorden delay \(O_Q(\logγ)\).

title: Discrete quantum Gaussians and central limit theorem
abstract: We introduce a quantum convolution and a conceptual framework to study states in discrete-variable (DV) quantum systems. All our results suggest that stabilizer states play a role in DV quantum systems similar to the role that Gaussian states play in continuous-variable systems. Hence we suggest the name ``discrete quantum Gaussians'' for stabilizer states. For example, we prove that the convolution of two stabilizer states is another stabilizer state, and that stabilizer states extremize both quantum entropy and Fisher information. We establish a ``maximal entropy principle,'' a ``second law of thermodynamics for quantum convolution,'' and a ``quantum central limit theorem.'' The latter is based on iterating the convolution of a zero-mean quantum state, which we prove converges to a stabilizer state. We bound the exponential rate of convergence of the quantum central limit theorem by the ``magic gap,'' defined in terms of the support of the characteristic function of the state. We elaborate on our general results with a discussion of some examples, as well as extending many of them to quantum channels.

Hence we suggest the name ``discrete quantum Gaussians'' for stabilizer states. For example, we prove that the convolution of two stabilizer states is another stabilizer state, and that stabilizer states extremize both quantum entropy and Fisher information. We establish a ``maximal entropy principle,'' a ``second law of thermodynamics for quantum convolution,'' and a ``quantum central limit theorem.'' The latter is based on iterating the convolution of a zero-mean quantum state, which we prove converges to a stabilizer state. We bound the exponential rate of convergence of the quantum central limit theorem by the ``magic gap,'' defined in terms of the support of the characteristic function of the state. We elaborate on our general results with a discussion of some examples, as well as extending many of them to quantum channels.

title: Constructing the Burrows-Wheeler Transform in Distributed Memory
abstract: The BURROWS-WHEELER TRANSFORM (BWT) [10] is an important fundamental algorithm in the world of string algorithms. It serves as the foundation of several algorithms [40, 6, 13], for example, text indices, enabling efficient string pattern matching [16]. The BWT is a permutation of the given string obtained by sorting all cyclic rotations of the string. The amount of genome data parsed using the BWT increases daily because of efforts like the GenomeTrakr network [22], which is collecting hundreds of thousands of genome sequences. Therefore, constructing the BWT for large datasets is of interest. There are multiple algorithms to construct the BWT [10, 51, 9, 14], some of which already focus on processing large amounts of data [9, 39, 11]. So far, there have not been efforts to develop BWT construction algorithms that use distributed high-performance computing systems. We present two distributed BWT construction algorithms. One adapts the traditional approach of constructing the BWT by computing the suffix array [43] in distributed memory. The other distributed algorithm is based on BIG-BWT [9], a BWT construction algorithm that uses PREFIX-FREE PARSING [9] as a preprocessing step. We modified the BIG-BWT algorithm to efficiently and scalably work in distributed memory. We show that both of our distributed BWT construction algorithms can scale up to 6144 cores. This makes them, to the best of our knowledge, the first distributed BWT construction algorithms to do so. This enables us to use more computation resources to construct the BWT. Our distributed PFP-based algorithm requires only 96 cores to match or surpass the runtime of the stateof-the-art shared-memory parallel BWT construction based on Lyndon words [51] running on a single 48-core compute node. Using 64x more cores, our distributed PFP-based construction algorithm achieves a speedup of up to 20.9x over the Lyndon-based construction running on a single compute node.

title: A Conceptual Systems Theory: Information, Control, Adaptation, and Evidence-Bound Closure
abstract: Relationship to Existing Ideas This framework originates in the author's personal way of organising observations about the world and about systems. It is not presented as a claim of scholarly originality. Many of its components have clear counterparts in established fields, and the value of the framework may lie more in the way these ideas are brought together than in any individual concept. As an initial orientation, several parts appear to have parallels with existing traditions: The distinction between a system's actual state and what can be inferred from observations is closely related to the concept of observability in control theory. The emphasis on feedback, correction, and the controller's capacity to respond to system variation has connections with ideas developed in cybernetics, including work associated with W. Ross Ashby and Stafford Beer. The distinction between a physical carrier, detection, interpretation, and usable information can be viewed alongside ideas from information theory and semiotics, where transmission of signals and interpretation of meaning are treated as different problems. The idea of closure conditions - that a conclusion should only be treated as settled when specified conditions have been met - has conceptual parallels with approaches to warranted conclusions in epistemology, evidentiary reasoning, and engineering assurance. These parallels are not presented as a literature review or as claims of equivalence. They are simply reference points showing where this personal systems perspective appears to touch existing bodies of thought.

title: Quantum Entanglement Gradient Field (QEFG)
abstract: Quantum Entanglement Gradient Field (QEFG) presents a novel mathematical framework for understanding and manipulating the gradient field generated by quantum entanglement. This research explores a mathematically rigorous approach to quantifying and controlling this field, aiming to predict and manipulate the propagation of information through entangled systems. The core mechanism centers on the development of a generalized differential equation incorporating quantum statistics, providing a precise mechanism for information transfer. This work represents a significant advancement in our comprehension of entanglement and its potential applications in quantum communication and computation.

title: Adaptive Quantum Topology Calculation
abstract: This paper presents an innovative computational algorithm, termed "Adaptive Quantum Topology Calculation," designed to efficiently simulate and analyze complex topological systems. Traditional approaches often rely on static, pre-defined models, limiting the algorithm's capabilities. Our approach leverages the unique properties of adaptive quantum topology structures to achieve enhanced precision and speed in topological calculations. This work introduces a novel methodology utilizing quantum entanglement and superposition to dynamically adjust the computational parameters, optimizing the simulation process for complex systems. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm through several illustrative examples, showcasing improved accuracy and reduced computational complexity compared to conventional methods. The core mechanism hinges on the inherent adaptability of these structures, enabling a more nuanced and responsive exploration of topological landscapes.

title: Quantum Geometry Clustering
abstract: This paper introduces Quantum Geometry Clustering (QGC), a novel clustering algorithm based on the principles of quantum geometry. We propose a method that automatically discovers patterns and structures within data sets by leveraging quantum geometric properties. QGC aims to move beyond traditional clustering techniques by identifying subtle correlations and hidden relationships within the data, offering a powerful tool for data analysis and pattern recognition. The core mechanism involves generating a set of 'quantum clusters' that represent the most significant data points, allowing for a deeper understanding of the underlying data distribution. We demonstrate the effectiveness of QGC through illustrative examples and discuss its potential applications in various fields.

abstract: This paper presents a novel method for precisely locking geometric phases using entanglement, enabling the creation of complex, stable geometric patterns. We introduce a quantum entanglement correlation algorithm that maintains the state of geometric phases, allowing for manipulation and control beyond traditional methods. The algorithm's design incorporates a carefully constructed quantum entanglement correlation scheme to achieve robust phase-locking. This approach offers a fundamentally new pathway to geometric phase manipulation, potentially revolutionizing computational geometry and materials science.

title: Dimension Generalization and the Interaction of Quantum Entanglement
abstract: This paper explores the potential of leveraging quantum entanglement to facilitate the precise simulation of quantum phenomena within high-dimensional spaces. We propose a novel dimensionality extension technique, termed "Quantum Entanglement Self-Adaptation," that utilizes the inherent properties of quantum entanglement to dynamically adjust the dimensionality of the simulation, thereby mitigating the inherent errors associated with traditional dimensionality reduction techniques. The core mechanism of this approach centers around establishing a self-adaptive entanglement structure that adjusts the simulation space's geometry in response to the quantum state, offering a pathway towards more accurate and robust simulations. The resulting framework addresses the limitations of current methods by providing a fundamentally different approach to dimensionality extension, potentially unlocking new capabilities in quantum simulation.

title: Based on Time Constant Dynamic Adjustment of Quantum Circuit Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to quantum circuit optimization centered around dynamically adjusting time constants within quantum circuits. The core idea is to leverage the inherent time-dependent evolution of quantum states governed by time constants to optimize the circuit's performance. Traditional quantum circuit optimization methods often rely on static circuit designs, neglecting the ability to adapt to the evolving quantum state. We propose a mechanism where time constants are dynamically adjusted, effectively modulating the coupling strengths and controllability between qubits during their evolution. This dynamic adjustment aims to steer the quantum state towards a desired final state more efficiently, thereby enhancing the overall quantum computation process. We explore the theoretical framework and potential implications of this methodology, highlighting its potential advantages over existing static optimization techniques. The optimization strategy relies on a feedback loop, continuously monitoring the quantum state's evolution and adjusting the time constants accordingly. This iterative process aims to minimize the circuit's execution time and maximize the fidelity of the final result. Further investigation into the mathematical formulation and control strategies will be crucial in realizing the full potential of this dynamic approach.

title: Quantum Computing Through Adaptive Geometry
abstract: Quantum computing offers the potential for unprecedented computational power, but its implementation faces significant challenges regarding coherence, error correction, and scalability. This paper proposes a novel approach to quantum computation based on adaptive geometry, dynamically adjusting geometric transformations to enhance qubit coherence and stability. We explore a system where the qubit's state is continuously monitored and transformed, allowing for precise control over the quantum system. The core mechanism leverages a set of predefined transformations, which are dynamically adjusted based on the current state of the qubits, to mitigate noise and improve fidelity. This paper details the design of the adaptive geometry framework, its implementation, and preliminary results demonstrating significant improvements in coherence times and error rates compared to traditional approaches. The proposed method offers a promising pathway towards more robust and efficient quantum computation.

title: Non-Linear Topological Structures for Quantum Computing: Adaptive Topology Generation
abstract: Quantum computing holds immense potential for revolutionary advancements across numerous fields, from drug discovery to materials science. However, the current limitations of quantum algorithms are largely constrained by the inherent fragility of quantum states and the difficulty in creating complex, dynamically adaptable circuits. This paper explores a novel approach to quantum computing based on non-linear topological structures, proposing a framework that utilizes dynamic topology generation to create quantum circuits with complex and self-adaptive structures. We introduce a new method for constructing quantum circuits, leveraging the principles of topology to induce intricate and responsive topological phases within the circuits. The core mechanism focuses on building circuits that inherently evolve in response to external stimuli or internal quantum states, enabling the generation of intricate and complex quantum states. This innovation addresses a key challenge in quantum computing – the lack of inherent adaptability – and offers a promising path toward the development of more robust and versatile quantum algorithms.

title: Quantifying the Knowledge in Deep Neural Networks: An Overview
abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have proven to be extremely effective at learning a wide range of tasks. Due to their complexity and inexplicable internal state, DNNs are difficult to analyze. Several attempts to interpret their operation have been made, but analyzing them from the perspective of the knowledge encoded in their layers is a promising research direction. The purpose of this survey is two-fold: (a) to review the concept of DNN knowledge quantification and highlight it as an important near-future challenge, and (b) to provide a brief account of the scant existing methods attempting to actually quantify DNN knowledge.

title: Comparing two unpaired means
abstract: Abstract This chapter will also be key in understanding and interpreting the results of t-tests, particularly comparisons between two independent groups, i.e., with unpaired data. This type of test always depends on underlying assumptions because they exploit particular distributions, such as the t-distribution in this case. We will delve into preliminary tests of normality and equality of variances, also called homoscedasticity. The latter will be an opportunity to use a new distribution to calculate a critical value and an alpha value. We will then get to the heart of the matter by starting with explaining what a t-ratio is and how to calculate it using different methods. The t-distribution studied previously will take on its full meaning here. The SciPy, statsmodels, and Pingouin libraries will once again be our best allies for performing these tests and determining confidence intervals. We will use a new dataset of Palmer penguins to perform t-tests in real-life case studies. The second part will be dedicated to the non-parametric Mann-Whitney U method as well as bootstrapping and permutation tests. The latter exploits the full programming potential of Python to generate pseudo-random samples from the original samples, demonstrating to be an accessible and interesting alternative to parametric and classical non-parametric t-tests.

title: The Normalization of Deviance in AI Development
abstract: Work on the risks of artificial intelligence has focused predominantly on capability risk: the danger that systems become too powerful, too autonomous, or too misaligned with human values. Far less attention has been paid to the organizational level---to whether the institutions building these systems are themselves predisposed to drift toward failure. This paper argues that they are. Regardless of how capable AI systems become, the organizations building them face the same structural dynamics that preceded past major technological disasters. Drawing on case studies of the Space Shuttle Challenger, the Three Mile Island accident, and the Boeing 737 MAX crashes, this paper identifies the common structural mechanisms preceding each failure and maps them onto contemporary AI development. The findings suggest that existing safety infrastructure may provide less protection than it appears, as organizations can complete safety processes in full compliance and still produce catastrophic outcomes. The pre-disaster period of AI development is still underway; the purpose of this paper is to make these dynamics legible while they can still be interrupted.

title: Quantum Entanglement Computing Field Simulation
abstract: Quantum Entanglement Computing Field Simulation is a novel computational approach that leverages the unique properties of quantum entanglement to simulate complex physical fields. Traditional computational methods struggle to accurately model phenomena involving entanglement, presenting a significant challenge for scientific and engineering applications. This paper proposes a new algorithm utilizing entangled qubits to transform the computation process, aiming to achieve higher precision and faster execution compared to conventional methods. We detail the core mechanism, explore its potential benefits, and discuss the challenges and future directions of this innovative approach.

title: 基于自适应的机器学习的动态模型调整
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic model adjustment method based on adaptive machine learning. Traditional model parameter adjustment methods often rely on fixed parameters, failing to effectively adapt to the dynamic nature of the simulated process. Our approach leverages an adaptive algorithm to dynamically adjust model parameters, ultimately enhancing model performance. We present a framework that systematically monitors data features and adjusts parameters to achieve optimal results. The core mechanism involves an iterative adjustment process guided by data distribution analysis, leading to improved model accuracy and generalization. This work offers a significant advancement in model optimization, particularly when dealing with complex, non-stationary data.

title: Title: Dynamic Fractal Geometry for Optimization of Machine Learning Algorithms
abstract: This paper investigates the integration of dynamic fractal geometry into machine learning algorithms to enhance performance and generalization. Traditional optimization methods often rely on fixed parameter settings, limiting the algorithm's adaptability. We propose a novel framework that utilizes an iterative process of fractal refinement, guided by the algorithm's performance metrics, to dynamically adjust parameters and improve model robustness. This approach addresses the limitations of static optimization techniques by providing a self-optimizing system. The core mechanism centers on the creation of fractal representations of the input data, allowing for a continuous, adaptive adjustment of the model's parameters. This study demonstrates the efficacy of this framework through simulations and a preliminary analysis of a standard machine learning task, showcasing improved generalization performance and faster convergence.

title: Quantum–Temporal Devices in the Carlo Field: A Full-Max Engineering Blueprint for Temporal Qubits, Time‑Biased Sensors, and Loop‑Cancelled Quantum Memory
abstract: This document presents the first complete engineering canon for **Quantum–Temporal Devices** built on the Carlo Field, treating temporal curvature, shear, loop geometry, and singularity mapping as first‑class design primitives. It defines the mathematical operators required for quantum–temporal evolution, extends the Hamiltonian with curvature, shear, and loop feedback terms, and establishes a full taxonomy of Quantum–Temporal Devices (QTDs). Three flagship technologies are developed to maximal depth: - Temporal Qubits (TQ): Qubits whose evolution is shaped by Carlo curvature, temporal shear, and loop interaction, enabling exotic gate operations and time‑reshaped algorithms. - Time‑Biased Sensors (TBS): Measurement devices that use temporal shear to bias sampling toward future or past states without violating causality. - Loop‑Cancelled Quantum Memory (LCQM): Memory architectures that detect harmful feedback loops and apply Carlo reset operators to suppress decoherence and extend coherence lifetimes. The document includes full mathematical derivations, device architectures, hardware and software stacks, safety and singularity‑avoidance constraints, and a phased roadmap for simulation, prototyping, and integration into a unified Quantum–Temporal Platform. This blueprint establishes the foundation for next‑generation quantum technologies that operate directly on engineered temporal geometry. KeywordsCarlo Field, Quantum–Temporal Devices, Temporal Qubits, Time‑Biased Sensors, Loop‑Cancelled Quantum Memory, Temporal Shear, Curvature Engineering, Singularity Mapping, Quantum Control, Quantum Architecture, Temporal Geometry, Quantum Information, Carlo Operators, Advanced Quantum Systems, Quantum Physics, Quantum Information Science, Theoretical Physics, Applied Mathematics, Computational Physics, Quantum Engineering, Temporal Dynamics, Field Theory, Advanced Device Architecture, Nonlinear Systems, Quantum Control Systems This open-access compendium contains a self-contained proof-of-concept visualizer, it provides an interactive exploration of the Carlo Field Quantum–Temporal framework. The package features a production-ready single-file HTML application complete with KaTeX-rendered mathematical notation, dynamic parameter sliders, and real-time WebGL/Canvas rendering models. It dynamically simulates and visualizes core architectural modes—including Temporal Qubits (TQ) shaped by gravitational-temporal curvature and shear fields, Time-Biased Sensors (TBS) demonstrating weighted sampling windows, and Loop-Cancelled Quantum Memories (LCQM) illustrating phase-noise stabilization and error cancellation. Designed to bridge formal systems architecture with tangible visual verification, the archive serves as a fully auditable reference implementation for non-linear temporal dynamics and quantum state evolution. title: Quantum Phase Field Optimization
abstract: Quantum Phase Field Optimization (QPFO) is a novel optimization algorithm that leverages the unique properties of quantum phase fields to automatically optimize complex physical systems. Traditional optimization methods often rely on empirical models and mathematical frameworks, offering limited adaptability to intricate systems. This paper introduces QPO, a groundbreaking algorithm utilizing quantum phase fields as a core optimization target, employing quantum algorithms to dynamically adjust parameters and achieve superior performance. We demonstrate QPO's effectiveness through a comprehensive analysis and preliminary experimental validation, highlighting its potential to revolutionize the optimization of advanced physical systems.

title: C2Trace
abstract: C2Trace is an auditable retrieval‑augmented framework for encrypted C2 traffic detection and family‑level attribution. It builds a multi‑view evidence matrix storing packet‑length, temporal and flow‑statistical evidence. A confidence gate routes only ambiguous samples to LLM arbitration with deterministic output verification. It supports adding new evidence without retraining, achieving traceable malicious traffic analysis with reduced inference overhead.

title: Title: Intrinsic Quantum Error Correction with Feedback Loops
abstract: Quantum computing holds immense promise for revolutionary advancements across numerous fields, but its inherent fragility necessitates robust error correction techniques. Current quantum error correction protocols, while effective, often rely on computationally intensive and potentially slow correction cycles. This research investigates a novel approach to intrinsic quantum error correction utilizing feedback loops, dynamically adjusting correction parameters to mitigate error rates in real-time. We propose a 'error detection and correction' loop that monitors the error rate and adjusts the correction strategy, offering a potential paradigm shift in error mitigation and paving the way for more practical and scalable quantum systems. This work demonstrates the feasibility of this approach through simulation and preliminary experimental validation, highlighting its potential to significantly reduce error rates and enhance the overall performance of quantum computations.

title: Self-Correcting Digital Circuits via Quantum-Inspired Entanglement-Based Feedback
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to self-correcting digital circuits utilizing quantum-inspired principles, specifically entanglement-based feedback. Traditional digital circuit error correction techniques often rely on redundancy and complex decoding algorithms, which can be computationally intensive and energy-consuming. This work proposes a circuit architecture that leverages entangled qubits to dynamically adjust circuit parameters in real-time, mimicking quantum interference to effectively mitigate the impact of noise and errors. The core mechanism involves designing a feedback loop where entangled qubits act as sensors and actuators, continuously monitoring and correcting the circuit's state. Mathematical models are presented to illustrate the principles and potential performance of this approach. The proposed method represents a fundamentally different paradigm for error correction, offering a potentially more efficient and robust solution for digital circuits. Key performance metrics such as error correction probability, latency, and energy consumption are discussed. The research contributes to the growing field of quantum-inspired computing and its application to practical digital circuit design.

title: Quantum Noise-Based Communication Protocol Security Authentication
abstract: This paper proposes a novel communication protocol security authentication scheme leveraging the inherent randomness of quantum noise. The core claim is to enhance communication security by exploiting this randomness for key generation, information encryption, and ultimately, secure authentication. The proposed mechanism involves designing a protocol where quantum noise is intentionally introduced during key exchange and transmission, fundamentally disrupting traditional cryptographic attacks reliant on predictable patterns. Statistical analysis of the noise patterns then forms the basis for the authentication process, creating a robust and resilient security layer. The novelty lies in moving beyond traditional cryptographic assumptions and directly utilizing the unpredictable nature of quantum phenomena for security. This approach offers a potential defense against attacks that target vulnerabilities in classical cryptographic systems. The paper details the protocol design, focusing on the mathematical formulation of the key generation, encryption, and authentication processes, highlighting the critical role of noise parameters and statistical analysis.

title: Title: Temporal Dynamics of Adaptive Neural Networks
abstract: This paper explores the concept of Temporal Dynamics of Adaptive Neural Networks (TDAN). Traditional neural network training often relies on fixed parameters and static updates. We propose a novel approach to training utilizing a reinforcement learning algorithm to dynamically adjust network weights based on the temporal evolution of the input data. This dynamic adaptation aims to improve the network's ability to learn complex patterns and generalize to unseen data. The core mechanism involves a reinforcement learning agent that steers the network's learning process, fostering a continuous refinement of its internal representation. This work presents a framework for adaptive learning with enhanced robustness and potential for improved performance across various tasks. The investigation will focus on the design of an agent capable of effectively capturing and responding to temporal changes in the input data. We will analyze the impact of the proposed dynamic adaptation strategy on the network's learning speed, accuracy, and generalization capabilities. The study will also examine the theoretical implications of the proposed approach, exploring its convergence properties and potential for further refinement.

title: Nonlinear regression
abstract: Abstract In this chapter, we will move on to nonlinear regression, which is used to model relationships that follow a curve rather than a straight line, as in many biological phenomena, such as those that can be described by the Hill equation. The complexity of this type of regression makes it impossible to solve by algebra, as with OLS, and requires an iterative process, that is, the algorithm is provided with initial parameters, or guesses, and optimizes the model parameters step-by-step until improving the fit is no longer possible. We will use a new specialized library for this process, lmfit, which allows us to set constraints and parameter limits, generates comprehensive diagnostic and statistical results, and offers comprehensive visualization tools. We will also discuss confidence bands, predictions, parameter space, and bootstrapping. Finally, we will see that it is possible to compare two nested nonlinear models using the techniques learned in the previous chapter.

The complexity of this type of regression makes it impossible to solve by algebra, as with OLS, and requires an iterative process, that is, the algorithm is provided with initial parameters, or guesses, and optimizes the model parameters step-by-step until improving the fit is no longer possible. We will use a new specialized library for this process, lmfit, which allows us to set constraints and parameter limits, generates comprehensive diagnostic and statistical results, and offers comprehensive visualization tools. We will also discuss confidence bands, predictions, parameter space, and bootstrapping. Finally, we will see that it is possible to compare two nested nonlinear models using the techniques learned in the previous chapter.

title: A Multi-Source Ensemble Approach to Candidate Generation for Alternative Vacation Rental Property Recommendations
abstract: Alternative property recommendations play a critical role in vacation rental marketplaces, helping users discover relevant options when viewing a specific listing. However, generating high-quality candidate alternatives presents unique challenges: heterogeneous inventory, geographic constraints, rapid availability changes, and long-tail property distributions. We present a comprehensive study of candidate generation (CG) approaches for vacation rental alternatives, comparing collaborative filtering, shallow embeddings, and graph neural network (GNN) methods. Our experiments on a large-scale vacation rental platform (over 2M active properties) show that a hybrid architecture combining item-based collaborative filtering with GNN-based retrieval improves Recall@300 by 14.8% over the strongest baseline, by leveraging the complementary strengths of the two sources: collaborative filtering excels at early recall for properties with rich interaction history, while GNNs discover diverse, non-obvious alternatives and handle cold-start scenarios more effectively. As a component result, GNN-based embeddings alone substantially outperform shallow Hotel2Vec embeddings (48-68% relative recall improvement across K), motivating their inclusion in the ensemble. Crucially, we examine how CG-stage gains carry through to the downstream ranking stage, and find that a stronger candidate pool yields higher downstream ranking quality, though attributing this effect cleanly is complicated by the coupling between candidate generation and ranker training. This recall-conversion gap is an important consideration for practitioners deploying new retrieval methods in two-stage recommendation systems.

title: Commonsense Reasoning in Computer Vision: Foundations, Recent Advancements, and Future Directions
abstract: Commonsense reasoning in computer vision encompasses integrating visual data and contextual knowledge, crucial for enhancing AI's understanding of everyday scenarios. This understanding not only improves machine learning models but also enhances their ability to interact meaningfully with humans and the environment. Unlike CNN-based conventional vision models, which are designed to identify objects within a specific image, incorporating commonsense knowledge enables models to interpret scenes in a more holistic manner, thereby improving their spatial ability to reason about relationships among objects and actions. This integration not only enhances object recognition but also facilitates a deeper understanding of the contextual factors, ultimately leading to more precise predictions and interactions in real-world applications. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of recent developments that integrate commonsense knowledge into computer vision tasks. We systematically review approaches based on knowledge graphs, scene graphs, neuro-symbolic models, and commonsense-augmented transformers. We also outline current limitations related to dataset bias, knowledge incompleteness, and integration challenges. Finally, we highlight prospective research trajectories in cross-modal reasoning, scalable commonsense knowledge injection, and neuro-symbolic hybrid architectures to develop truly intelligent visual systems.

title: RefDiT: Local Attribute Guidance in Reference-Based Image Generation
abstract: Personalization models generate new images guided by a few subject references, while style transfer methods aim to produce images aligned with a global style derived from a reference image. Recent approaches perform well when the reference image contains a single object, effectively capturing a global style that encompasses all implicit attributes. However, when applied to complex real-world scenes containing multiple objects with distinct attribute characteristics, these methods, due to their global-level guidance, fail to localize relevant elements in the reference image. The global guidance restricts their ability to generate new images based on the local attributes in the reference image. Moreover, existing methods typically employ a single identifier token to capture all details from the reference, resulting in a lack of individual, attribute-level control. Motivated by these limitations, we propose RefDiT, a novel framework for reference-guided image generation. RefDiT takes as input a reference image, a text prompt, and an optional user-provided guidance context. RefDiT employs local region guidance using the attributes of local elements. It constructs an attribute-aware conditioning signal from the reference image by performing attribute-level decomposition of the identifier token and performs context adjustment in the inference prompt to train low-rank adapter (LoRA) blocks of a diffusion transformer (DiT)-based generative model. RefDiT learns the correspondence between identifier tokens and local regions in the reference image, enabling more effective local guidance.

title: SeamFlow: Structure-Aware Flow Matching on Edge Probabilities for Artist-Like UV Unwrapping
abstract: 3D surface cutting and UV unwrapping are fundamental problems in computer graphics. Traditional geometric optimization methods mainly focus on reducing parameterization distortion, but they often overlook visual semantic coherence in seam layouts. Recent autoregressive generative methods improve semantic coherence, yet limited perception of mesh topology often causes inaccurate local cuts. To address these limitations, we introduce SeamFlow, a novel generative framework for 3D surface cutting. We reformulate the discrete mesh-cutting problem as continuous flow matching in a high-dimensional edge-probability space. Through continuous relaxation, SeamFlow learns a deterministic mapping from a Gaussian prior to a target seam-probability distribution. An evolution network couples local topological tokens with global shape priors and guides smooth probability flow through Ordinary Differential Equation solving. Compared with existing autoregressive generative frameworks, SeamFlow improves topology awareness through edge tokenization while eliminating both 3D spatial projection errors and artificial sequential-order bias. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SeamFlow achieves exceptional semantic coherence and remarkably low parameterization distortion. The project page is https://meshy-dev.github.io/seamflow.

title: Few-shot neuromorphic vision in a nonlinear photonic network laser
abstract: With the growing prevalence of artificial intelligence (AI), demand increases for hardware that mimics the brain's ability to extract structure from limited data. In the retina, ganglion cells detect features from sparse inputs via lateral inhibition, where neurons antagonistically suppress activity of neighboring cells. Biological neurons exhibit diverse heterogeneous nonlinear responses, linked to robust learning and strong performance in low-data regimes. Here, we introduce a retinally inspired photonic computing system where spatially competing lasing modes in a random network laser act as heterogeneous, inhibitively coupled neurons, enabling feature detection, few-shot classification, and segmentation. This silicon-compatible scheme harnesses heterogeneous excitatory and inhibitory nonlinear physical dynamics, which give rise to emergent photonic computing behavior, including parallel feature detection and strong performance when training data are scarce. We report 98.05 and 87.85% accuracy on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, and 90.12% on BreakHis cancer diagnosis, outperforming software convolutional neural networks including EfficientNetV2 and the vision transformer ViT in few-shot and class-imbalanced regimes with training sets of up to several hundred images. We demonstrate combined segmentation and classification on the HAM10k skin lesion dataset, achieving DICE and Jaccard scores of 84.49 and 74.80%. These results demonstrate the potential of random lasing networks as nonlinear photonic learning systems and highlight the ability of heterogeneous nonlinear dynamics to support strong learning in challenging low-data scenarios.

title: Penerapan Deep Learning (Artificial Neural Network) Untuk Klasifikasi Diagnostik Kanker Payudara Guna Mendukung Efisiensi Biaya Deteksi Dini
abstract: Kanker payudara merupakan salah satu jenis kanker dengan insiden tertinggi pada perempuan di Indonesia, dan lebih dari separuh pasien di rumah sakit rujukan kanker masih terdiagnosis pada stadium lanjut, sehingga biaya pengobatan yang harus ditanggung menjadi jauh lebih tinggi dibandingkan penanganan pada stadium awal. Deteksi dini yang cepat dan akurat menjadi kunci untuk menekan biaya pengobatan sekaligus meningkatkan peluang kesembuhan pasien. Penelitian ini bertujuan merancang dan mengevaluasi model deep learning berbasis Artificial Neural Network (Multi-Layer Perceptron) untuk mengklasifikasikan tumor payudara ke dalam kategori jinak (benign) dan ganas (malignant). Penelitian menggunakan dataset Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer (WDBC) yang terdiri atas 569 sampel dan 30 fitur numerik, dibagi menjadi 455 data latih dan 114 data uji (80:20) secara stratified. Model ANN dengan tiga lapisan tersembunyi (64-32-16 neuron) dievaluasi menggunakan akurasi, presisi, recall, F1-score, dan AUC serta dibandingkan dengan Logistic Regression, Random Forest, dan Support Vector Machine. Hasil menunjukkan Deep Neural Network mencapai akurasi 97,37%, presisi 97,26%, recall 98,61%, F1-score 97,93%, dan AUC 0,995, sementara Logistic Regression dan SVM mencapai akurasi 98,25%. Hasil ini menunjukkan bahwa model Deep Neural Network tidak mengungguli model klasik pada data tabular berukuran kecil. Pendekatan ini berpotensi mendukung skrining kanker payudara sebagai alat bantu diagnosis, sedangkan efisiensi biaya masih memerlukan analisis cost-effectiveness formal.

title: Title: Multi-Scale Bayesian Inference for Signal Processing
abstract: This paper presents a novel Bayesian inference framework designed for multi-scale signal processing. Traditional approaches often treat signal processing as a series of individual analysis steps, neglecting the crucial interplay between different scales. Our work introduces a "Multi-Scale Bayesian Filtering" – a system that simultaneously analyzes data at multiple levels of abstraction, creating a hierarchical representation of the signal. This allows for a more comprehensive understanding of signal propagation and improved accuracy in estimating and modeling signal characteristics. The framework incorporates hierarchical Bayesian models to effectively capture the dependencies between different scales, leading to a more robust and accurate solution than conventional methods. The core mechanism involves applying Bayesian inference at varying levels of abstraction, resulting in a unified representation of the signal.

title: Title: Hierarchical Quantum State Collapse with Feedback
abstract: Quantum state collapse is a fundamental process in quantum mechanics, and its inherent instability presents significant challenges to quantum computing and quantum information processing. Traditional collapse mechanisms often rely on purely random fluctuations, leading to errors and hindering the development of reliable quantum systems. This paper proposes a novel hierarchical quantum state collapse process, designed to enhance stability and reduce errors through the implementation of a structured hierarchy. The core mechanism centers around a system where each level of the hierarchy is responsible for collapsing a subset of the data, ensuring that the collapse is guided by the structure of the data. This approach offers a promising pathway to mitigate noise and instability, potentially leading to more robust and reliable quantum systems.

title: Bayesian Differential Geometry for Dynamical Systems
abstract: This paper presents a novel Bayesian differential geometry approach to formulating and solving differential equations, specifically tailored for systems with complex, non-linear dynamics and inherent uncertainty. Traditional methods often rely on analytical solutions, which are rarely applicable to real-world systems. Our method leverages a Bayesian framework, dynamically updating probability distributions based on observational data to determine the solution path. We introduce a new adaptive algorithm that incorporates the system's uncertainty, offering a powerful tool for modeling and analyzing dynamic systems across diverse fields. The core mechanism centers around Bayesian inference, using a hierarchical Bayesian structure to represent the system's state and evolve over time. This approach eliminates the need for explicit parameter estimation, significantly simplifying the process and enhancing the model's robustness. The paper details the algorithm's implementation, provides a comprehensive analysis of its performance, and discusses potential applications in various disciplines.

title: 基于自适应量子纠错的相位调整策略
abstract: Quantum entanglement is a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, offering the potential for secure communication and powerful computation. However, quantum systems are highly susceptible to environmental noise, leading to errors in quantum operations. Quantum error correction is a critical area of research focused on mitigating these errors. This paper introduces a novel approach to quantum error correction – a dynamic phase adjustment strategy – leveraging adaptive quantum entanglement. We propose a "Quantum Phase Evolution" mechanism that continuously monitors and adjusts the phase of individual qubits in response to observed errors. This dynamic adjustment allows the system to self-correct errors more effectively than traditional methods, potentially leading to improved fidelity and scalability. This work explores the impact of this dynamic phase adjustment on the overall performance of quantum systems.

title: Dynamic Constraint Propagation in Neural Network Training
abstract: This paper investigates a novel dynamic constraint propagation technique for neural network training. Traditional training methods often rely on fixed constraints, which can lead to overfitting and poor generalization. This work proposes a mechanism to continuously adjust constraint propagation based on the model's performance, effectively mitigating these issues. We introduce a feedback loop that analyzes the model's error during training and iteratively refines the constraint distribution, resulting in improved accuracy and robustness. The core of this approach is a novel algorithm that leverages a gradient-based approach coupled with a constraint propagation rule that adapts to the training process. The resultant model exhibits significantly enhanced generalization capabilities compared to static constraint propagation methods.

title: Quantum Time-Scale Calibration (QTSC)
abstract: This paper introduces Quantum Time-Scale Calibration (QTSC), a novel system designed to calibrate time scales within quantum systems by correlating them with specific geometric patterns. The core mechanism leverages a "Geometric Time-Scale Resonance" technique, dynamically linking time intervals to the fundamental geometry of the quantum system, thereby enhancing the predictability of quantum behavior. QTSC offers a significant improvement over existing calibration methods, providing a pathway to establish precise time scales and unlock a deeper understanding of quantum phenomena.

title: Quantum Entanglement Parallel Computing Paradigm
abstract: This paper investigates a novel paradigm for parallel computation predicated on the principles of quantum entanglement. The core claim is the development of a framework that leverages entanglement to enable efficient data transfer and computation across multiple processing units, offering a potential breakthrough in tackling large-scale computational challenges. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of this approach, detail the implementation of a preliminary system, and discuss future research directions aimed at maximizing its potential.

title: Multi-Agent Collaborative Task Planning for Robot Systems
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to robot task planning leveraging the power of multi-agent collaboration. Traditional robot task planning methods often struggle with complex scenarios requiring coordination between multiple robots, leading to sub-optimal solutions. Our approach utilizes a reinforcement learning (RL)-based multi-agent collaborative algorithm to enable robots to learn effective cooperation strategies. The core claim of this work is that multi-agent collaborative robot task planning should effectively exploit the strengths and weaknesses of each individual agent. The central mechanism involves a distributed learning framework where agents interact and refine their behavior through trial and error, ultimately achieving complex task completion. This represents a significant advancement over conventional methods, offering a dynamic and adaptable solution for multi-robot systems. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of the algorithm and present a conceptual framework for its implementation. The focus is on a generalizable architecture that can be adapted to various task domains and robot configurations. The key innovations include the decentralized nature of the learning process and the ability of agents to dynamically adjust their strategies based on the evolving environment and the actions of their peers. The results, while presented conceptually here due to the absence of experimental validation, demonstrate the potential of this approach to achieve superior performance compared to traditional, centralized planning methods.

title: Neurobiological Plasticity Programming Model
abstract: This paper presents a biologically-inspired programming model designed to leverage the principles of neuronal plasticity, specifically long-term potentiation (LTP) and long-term depression (LTD), to achieve self-optimization and adaptation to complex tasks. The model simulates the dynamic changes associated with LTP/LTD through feedback and competitive mechanisms, resulting in the formation and elimination of connections within a neural network, mirroring biological neural structures. The core claim is that by directly incorporating these plasticity mechanisms, we can create a system capable of continuous learning and adaptation. The model's architecture is based on a recurrent network with adjustable synaptic weights, and the learning rules are governed by the classic Hebbian learning principle, modified to account for the temporal dynamics of LTP and LTD. Simulation results demonstrate the model's ability to learn and adapt to novel environments and tasks. The key innovation lies in the dynamic and adaptive nature of the network, which is fundamentally driven by the simulated plasticity mechanisms. Further research will explore scaling the model and investigating its performance on more complex cognitive tasks.

title: Dynamically Weighted Graph Neural Networks for Multi-Task Learning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to multi-task learning utilizing dynamically weighted Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Traditional GNNs often fail to effectively transfer knowledge between different tasks due to their reliance on static graph structures. We propose a framework where the message passing process is dynamically weighted based on the relevance of each node to the current task. This adaptive weighting mechanism allows the GNN to prioritize relevant information, thereby enhancing knowledge transfer and improving performance across multiple tasks. The core idea involves learning a task-specific weighting function for each node, modulating the influence of neighboring nodes during message aggregation. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, showcasing improved performance compared to standard GNNs in multi-task learning scenarios. The key contribution lies in providing a mechanism for adaptive knowledge transfer within GNNs, directly addressing a significant challenge in multi-task learning applications.

title: Title: Adaptive Wave Function Collapse with Deterministic Control
abstract: Quantum computation, a fundamentally new paradigm of computation, relies on the manipulation of quantum states through wave function collapse. While probabilistic wave function collapse provides a basis for quantum mechanics, it often lacks precision in achieving desired outcomes. This paper explores a novel approach to wave function collapse – Adaptive Wave Function Collapse with Deterministic Control – designed to enhance the precision of quantum computation. We introduce a 'Controlled Collapse Matrix,' a system that allows for precise, predictable manipulation of the collapse process, thereby enabling more accurate and controllable quantum states. The paper details the design and implementation of this matrix, demonstrating its ability to improve the fidelity of quantum measurements and explore potential applications in quantum algorithm design. We present preliminary results showcasing the benefits of this approach over traditional methods.

title: SQL-GRID: A Grounded Retrieval and Interactive Disambiguation Agent for Text-to-SQL over Power Grid Data
abstract: Power grid data often contain highly abstract metadata, ambiguous business terms, and complex statistical scopes. These characteristics make general large language models prone to semantic deviation and SQL hallucination in Text-to-SQL tasks. To address this problem, this paper proposes SQL-GRID, a grounded retrieval and interactive disambiguation agent for Text-to-SQL over power grid data. The framework is based on a multi-agent collaboration mechanism. It integrates retrieval, validation, disambiguation, and SQL generation modules to transform natural language intent into accurate SQL statements. To bridge the gap between business semantics and database structures, this paper constructs a Business Knowledge Representation(BKR) based knowledge base, which integrates database structural information, business descriptions, real data samples, and statistical rules. A multi-strategy RAG method is also designed. It combines semantic vector retrieval with keyword matching and provides accurate domain knowledge for SQL generation. To address business ambiguity, this paper further proposes a closed-loop mechanism consisting of pre-generation disambiguation, interactive clarification, and post-generation validation. Through explicit human-machine interaction, the framework guides users to clarify statistical granularity and statistical scope constraints. This process effectively reduces uncertainty during SQL generation. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves a metadata recall rate of 94% on the power grid dataset. The SQL execution rate increases from 40.2% in the traditional baseline to 84.6%. The semantic matching score reaches 4.85. These results show that the proposed framework significantly improves the accuracy and reliability of self-service queries in complex power grid scenarios.

title: Comparing Socratic Questioning to Explanatory and Correct Response Feedback
abstract: A growing consensus in the EdTech industry is that AI tutors should respond to errors with scaffolded questions rather than direct answers, prompting students to reason through problems interactively. The logic is compelling: active questioning prevents overreliance on the tutor, it may deepen engagement, expose hidden misconceptions, and allow the tutor to adapt in real time. However, Socratic questioning is also costly. Each back-and-forth exchange takes time, and students who cannot answer a probing question may find the experience more frustrating than illuminating. In this study we will test whether the interactivity of Socratic questioning adds value beyond personalization alone, comparing four feedback conditions in an online experiment involving mathematics problem-solving. Participants will practice setting up constraint equations and receive one of four types of feedback after incorrect responses: correctness-only feedback, a generic explanation of the correct answer, a personalized explanation targeting their specific error, or a Socratic dialogue that guides them through the problem in scaffolded steps. We will examine the impact of this manipulation on learning and measures of efficiency and motivation.

title: The Gaussian distribution
abstract: Abstract This chapter discusses the Gaussian distribution, a key concept in statistical analysis in general, since the various tests outlined throughout the book will be closely linked to it. We will see how to create a normal distribution object in Python and how to use it to calculate the different probabilities, such as the probability density function (PDF), cumulative density function (CDF), as well as the percent point function (PPF) and survival function (SF). It will also explain how to plot the distribution with the Matplotlib package, which will allow us to better understand the concepts of one- and two-tailed, critical values as well as that of the P value.

title: Reimagining breast cancer diagnosis with quantum technology
abstract: The impacts of breast cancer remain a severe cause of death, significantly affecting the quality of life, especially among women. Traditional diagnostic approaches, particularly in the early stages, lack sophistication, reliability, and accuracy. Early and accurate diagnosis is crucial for improving survival rates and reducing the need for aggressive treatments. To address this, QSVM-GSA, an innovative quantum algorithm, is proposed. This novel integrated quantum framework simultaneously addresses the dual challenge of high diagnostic accuracy (via QSVM's quantum kernel trick) and computational efficiency/speed (via GSA integration). QSVM-GSA combines the Quantum Support Vector Machine and Grover's Search Algorithm, leveraging quantum mechanics for superior diagnostic accuracy and efficiency. It encodes complex medical data, such as the Wisconsin Breast Cancer Dataset, into quantum states. QSVM operates in the exponentially larger Hilbert space, identifying subtle patterns missed by classical classifiers. Quantum kernels establish nuanced relationships within the data, enabling precise tumour classification. Grover's search accelerates this process, offering a quadratic speed gain in scanning vast datasets and optimising feature selection. This allows for rapid identification of malignant patterns without compromising accuracy. Robustness is enhanced through advanced error-correcting techniques, ensuring fault tolerance and preserving computational integrity even in noisy environments. The model achieved 84.4% accuracy, 83.3% precision, 88.2% recall, and 85.7% F1-score on the Wisconsin Breast Cancer Dataset. Ultimately, QSVM-GSA represents a significant breakthrough in medical diagnostics, setting new standards in accuracy, speed, and reliability for breast cancer detection.
